article_text:
SPOILERS: This post contains details about the VisionQuest Season 1 finale episode “Forever”

A major player appears to be returning to the MCU following the Season 1 finale of VisionQuest .

In a post-credits scene from Tuesday’s finale episode “Forever”, a hooded figure that appears to be Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom raises the rubble of Wundagore off Wanda Maximoff/Scarlet Witch ( Elizabeth Olsen ) after she seemingly killed herself under the collapsing mountain in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022).

“Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine,” says the hooded figure.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

‘VisionQuest’ Seems Eager To Confront Dangers Of Unregulated AI, But The Team Behind It Says MCU Series Isn’t A Reflection Of Current Events

What To Watch Before ‘VisionQuest’: From ‘Age Of Ultron’ To ‘WandaVision’

The post-credits scene seems to hint at Olsen’s return for Avengers: Doomsday , premiering Dec. 18 in theaters, after Vision (Paul Bettany) was reunited with both their sons, Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) and Billy (Joe Locke), in the finale, which follows the events of WandaVision (2021) and Agatha All Along (2024).

Marvel Studios hinted at the family potentially being fully reunited on social media ahead of Thursday’s finale, sharing a message in binary code that appears to translate to: “We could never truly leave each other, even if we tried.” Wanda previously said that to Tommy and Billy in the finale of WandaVision .

Meanwhile, Olsen has said “ I know nothing ” when asked about her character’s potential return to the MCU. “I don’t know what’s going on. It’s safer for me to not know anything because then I can’t make a mistake in a situation like this. I rather know nothing,” she said in March.

article_text:
アートを入口に、見慣れた公園の風景をあらためて見つめ直す 「Hibiya Art Park 2026 - Timeless Phenomena 確かにありそうなもの -」 が、11月13日から29日まで 日比谷公園 で開催される。建築家の 永山祐子 がディレクターを務め、 丹原健翔 をキュレトリアルコラボレーターに迎え、 栗林隆 、 佐々木類 、 横手太紀 の3名のアーティストが参加する。公園内に作品を点在させ、花や木々、光や風とともに新たな風景を作り出す。

東京都が実施する「花と光のムーブメント」の一環として開催される本イベント。今年のテーマは「Timeless Phenomena 確かにありそうなもの」。開園から120年以上にわたり、東京の中心で都市の変化を見守ってきた日比谷公園には、街の喧騒とは異なる、植物や生き物、季節の移ろいが刻む時間が流れている。アートを通して、普段は見過ごしがちな自然の気配や、人間とほかの生き物との関係に目を向ける。

栗林隆は、自然と人間、可視と不可視など、様々な「境界」を主題にインスタレーションや映像作品を制作してきた。《日比谷の樹 Tree of Hibiya》は、かつて海だった日比谷の土地の記憶や、人間の営みを内包する「樹」。内部に入る体験を通して、訪れる人に土地の歴史や未来について問いかける。

ガラスを主な素材に、身近な自然や生活環境から着想を得た作品を手がける佐々木類は、《透明な巣 Unseen Nest》を発表する。熱したガラスを糸のように自らの身体の周囲へと垂らし、身体の大きさや動き、制作時の感情までを刻み込んだ。透明なガラスが公園の自然や周囲の風景とどのように調和するのかにも注目したい。

横手太紀は、《All We Imagine as Light, Gathered Around a Light》で花々に囲まれた「公園の中の公園」のような空間を創出。公園で実際に使われている工業製品やレジャーシートの素材を用いた、ゆっくりと動く彫刻を設置する。幻想的な花畑のようでありながら、自然と人工物が入り混じる風景によって、人間や動物、虫、植物など、異なるリズムで生きる存在が同じ場所を共有する様子を表現する。

会期中には、 花崎草 による参加型パフォーマンス《花束往還（はなたばおうかん）》も実施される。公園に現れる花束の屋台で、参加者は花束の包み紙の表に自分自身の願いを、裏にはその願いを見知らぬ誰かへの祈りに書き換えた言葉を記し、ドライフラワーとともに包んで並べる。その代わりに、別の人が作った花束をひとつ持ち帰るというもの。花束を介して、見知らぬ人同士の思いが行き交う。

また、会場にはBLUE BOTTLE COFFEE、DAN Curry、sabasu、TRUFFLE Bakery、hammamなどが出店するフードマーケットも登場する。さらに、11月13日から15日までの3日間、 東京ミッドタウン日比谷 ではアート、クラフト、フード＆ドリンクを軸とした約40組のショップ・クリエイターが集結するマーケットイベント 「SUPER ART & CRAFT MARKET 2026」 も開催される。倉中るな・尾形凌によるワークショップや、こけしの絵付けを楽しめる「オープンスタジオ」のほか、Hibiya Art Park 2026との連携企画もあり、こちらも見逃せない。

公園と街を巡りながら、目には見えなくてもたしかにそこにある、自然や他者とのつながりを見つめ直す機会となりそうだ。

title_original: Wem gehört Frida Kahlos Kunst?
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Gelman-Sammlung mit 18 Werken von Frida Kahlo ist nach jahrelanger Abwesenheit erstmals wieder in Europa zu sehen. In Mexiko sorgt der Umzug nach Spanien für Proteste. Dahinter steht auch eine grundsätzliche Frage: Wem gehört das kulturelle Erbe eines Landes?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Im Frühjahr sorgten Proteste in Mexiko für Schlagzeilen , die sich gegen die Verlegung der Gelman-Sammlung nach Santander in Spanien richteten. Wegen Erbstreitigkeiten war sie 20 Jahre lang nicht in Mexiko zu sehen gewesen. Erst Anfang dieses Jahres wurde sie in der viel besuchten Ausstellung \"Modern Stories: The Emblematic Works from the Gelman Santander Collection\" im Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexiko-Stadt wieder gezeigt. Die Nachricht von ihrem geplanten Umzug löste daraufhin Empörung aus. In einem Gastbeitrag für die \"New York Times\" bezeichnete der mexikanische Historiker Francisco Berzunza den Vorgang als \"Plünderung unter anderem Namen\". Präsidentin Claudia Sheinbaum versprach, sich für die Rückkehr der Werke nach Mexiko einzusetzen.", "links": [{"text": "für Schlagzeilen", "url": "https://www.monopol-magazin.de/kahlo-werke-kehren-2028-nach-mexiko-zurueck"}, {"text": "einem Gastbeitrag für die \"New York Times\"", "url": "https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/28/opinion/mexico-frida-kahlo-art.html"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ungeachtet der Kontroverse sind nun erstmals 95 Werke der Sammlung in Europa zu sehen: in der Ausstellung \"Modern Mexico in the Gelman Santander Collection\" im nordspanischen Santander. Wenig überraschend stehen Frida Kahlo und die faszinierenden Geschichten der Sammler Jacques und Natasha Gelman im Mittelpunkt – einschließlich der Debatte um den rechtmäßigen Verbleib der Sammlung. Doch wenn es darum geht, welche Erzählung hier am stärksten wirkt, geht Kahlo eindeutig als Siegerin hervor."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wie die Werke nach Santander kamen"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Empörung mexikanischer Kunstliebhaber über den Verlust ihres kulturellen Erbes ist nachvollziehbar. Die Sammlung umfasst zwar nur 160 Arbeiten, enthält aber zahlreiche Meisterwerke, darunter 18 Bilder von Kahlo. Die Malerin, die im Alter von 47 Jahren starb, nachdem sie mit 18 bei einem Autounfall schwer verletzt worden war, hinterließ allerdings nur 143 Gemälde – darunter 55 Selbstporträts. Zehn davon befanden sich im Besitz der Gelmans."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jacques Gelman wurde in Sankt Petersburg in eine wohlhabende jüdische Familie geboren, die vor der bolschewistischen Revolution floh. Er studierte Filmproduktion in Deutschland und lebte in Berlin und Paris, bevor er sich 1938 in Mexiko-Stadt niederließ. Natasha Gelman kam 1939 auf der Flucht vor den Nationalsozialisten nach Mexiko. Die beiden heirateten 1941. 1943 gründete Jacques gemeinsam mit anderen die Filmproduktionsfirma Posa Films. Mit Komödien und Verfilmungen westlicher Literaturklassiker machte er ein Vermögen – in einer künstlerisch besonders produktiven Phase, die als das Goldene Zeitalter des mexikanischen Kinos bekannt wurde."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Das Ehepaar kannte zahlreiche mexikanische Künstler persönlich, darunter Kahlo und Rivera, und kaufte Werke direkt von ihnen. Nach Jacques' Tod vermachte Natasha die Sammlung ihrem US-amerikanischen Freund, dem Kurator Robert Littman. Ihr Testament wurde von ihrer Familie erfolglos angefochten. Littman verkaufte die Sammlung 2023 an die in Monterrey ansässige Industriellenfamilie Zambrano. Diese nutzte die Werke anschließend als Sicherheit für einen Kredit der Santander-Bank – so gelangte die Sammlung nach Spanien."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Porträts Natashas spiegeln ihren Wohlstand"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Im Faro Santander wird Jacques' Leidenschaft für das Kino anhand zahlreicher Schwarz-Weiß-Fotografien und -Filmstills erzählt. Besonders eindrucksvoll sind die mythisch aufgeladenen Landschaftsaufnahmen und die düsteren urbanen Szenen des gefeierten Kameramanns des Goldenen Zeitalters, Gabriel Figueroa, mit dem Gelman an einigen Filmproduktionen zusammenarbeitete. Zusammen mit Lola Álvarez Bravos fotojournalistischen Einblicken in das städtische Leben und den formalistischen Aufnahmen von Manuel Álvarez Bravo verdeutlichen die Werke die stilistische Vielfalt der modernen mexikanischen Fotografie."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Porträts Natashas in der Ausstellung spiegeln den Wohlstand und die Kunstförderung des Ehepaars. Das Bildnis von Kahlo fällt überraschend kühl aus: Es zeigt Gelman als eisige slawische Schönheit, in Pelz gehüllt und mit einem katzenhaften, leicht hochmütigen Ausdruck, der an die Porträts Alberto Giacomettis erinnert. Riveras Porträt – obwohl im selben Jahr entstanden, zeigt es sie schmeichelhaft jünger – stellt Gelman lasziv auf einem Sofa dar. Der Schlitz ihres weißen Kleides gibt den Blick auf ihre langen, wohlgeformten Beine frei. In der Vitrine neben dem Gemälde ist die mit Diamanten besetzte Brosche zu sehen, die Gelman während der Porträtsitzung trug."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://monopol-prod.nbg1.your-objectstorage.com/s3fs-public/styles/max1560x1150/public/2026-11/6.%20Diego%20Rivera.%20Retrato%20de%20Natasha%20Gelman.jpeg?itok=YPkpVVQb", "alt": "Diego Rivera, Retrato de Natasha Gelman, Gemälde: Frau im weißen Kleid vor Calla-Lilien, liegend.", "caption": "© 2026 Banco de México Diego & Rivera Frida Kahlo Museums Trust. Av. 5 de Mayo No. 2, col. Centro, alc. Cuauhtémoc, c.p. 06000, Mexico City; VG Bildkunst. Diego Rivera, Portrait of Natasha Gelman , 1943", "credit": "Monopol"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rivera selbst ist die zentrale Figur der Ausstellung. Die gezeigten Werke zeichnen seine künstlerische Entwicklung nach: von frühen kubistischen Arbeiten wie \"Last Hour\" (1915) bis zu traumartigen Wüstenlandschaften wie \"Landscape with Cacti\" (1931). Während der späte Rivera vor allem für seine politischen Wandgemälde bekannt war, präsentiert die Ausstellung stattdessen ein kleineres Gemälde: \"Sunflowers\" (1943). Es zeigt zwei indigene Kinder beim Spielen, von denen eines eine weiße Puppe auseinanderreißt. Das Bild ist unverkennbar didaktisch angelegt, strahlt aber zugleich eine humanistische Wärme aus."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ein Schwarz-Weiß-Porträt von Richard Silberstein aus dem Jahr 1940 zeigt Rivera und Kahlo in einer Konstellation, in der er beinahe wie eine Vaterfigur wirkt. article_text:
Die Gelman-Sammlung mit 18 Werken von Frida Kahlo ist nach jahrelanger Abwesenheit erstmals wieder in Europa zu sehen. In Mexiko sorgt der Umzug nach Spanien für Proteste. Dahinter steht auch eine grundsätzliche Frage: Wem gehört das kulturelle Erbe eines Landes?

Im Frühjahr sorgten Proteste in Mexiko für Schlagzeilen , die sich gegen die Verlegung der Gelman-Sammlung nach Santander in Spanien richteten. Wegen Erbstreitigkeiten war sie 20 Jahre lang nicht in Mexiko zu sehen gewesen. Erst Anfang dieses Jahres wurde sie in der viel besuchten Ausstellung "Modern Stories: The Emblematic Works from the Gelman Santander Collection" im Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexiko-Stadt wieder gezeigt. Die Nachricht von ihrem geplanten Umzug löste daraufhin Empörung aus. In einem Gastbeitrag für die "New York Times" bezeichnete der mexikanische Historiker Francisco Berzunza den Vorgang als "Plünderung unter anderem Namen". Präsidentin Claudia Sheinbaum versprach, sich für die Rückkehr der Werke nach Mexiko einzusetzen.

Ungeachtet der Kontroverse sind nun erstmals 95 Werke der Sammlung in Europa zu sehen: in der Ausstellung "Modern Mexico in the Gelman Santander Collection" im nordspanischen Santander. Wenig überraschend stehen Frida Kahlo und die faszinierenden Geschichten der Sammler Jacques und Natasha Gelman im Mittelpunkt – einschließlich der Debatte um den rechtmäßigen Verbleib der Sammlung. Doch wenn es darum geht, welche Erzählung hier am stärksten wirkt, geht Kahlo eindeutig als Siegerin hervor.

Wie die Werke nach Santander kamen

Die Empörung mexikanischer Kunstliebhaber über den Verlust ihres kulturellen Erbes ist nachvollziehbar. Die Sammlung umfasst zwar nur 160 Arbeiten, enthält aber zahlreiche Meisterwerke, darunter 18 Bilder von Kahlo. Die Malerin, die im Alter von 47 Jahren starb, nachdem sie mit 18 bei einem Autounfall schwer verletzt worden war, hinterließ allerdings nur 143 Gemälde – darunter 55 Selbstporträts. Zehn davon befanden sich im Besitz der Gelmans.

Jacques Gelman wurde in Sankt Petersburg in eine wohlhabende jüdische Familie geboren, die vor der bolschewistischen Revolution floh. Er studierte Filmproduktion in Deutschland und lebte in Berlin und Paris, bevor er sich 1938 in Mexiko-Stadt niederließ. Natasha Gelman kam 1939 auf der Flucht vor den Nationalsozialisten nach Mexiko. Die beiden heirateten 1941. 1943 gründete Jacques gemeinsam mit anderen die Filmproduktionsfirma Posa Films. Mit Komödien und Verfilmungen westlicher Literaturklassiker machte er ein Vermögen – in einer künstlerisch besonders produktiven Phase, die als das Goldene Zeitalter des mexikanischen Kinos bekannt wurde.

Das Ehepaar kannte zahlreiche mexikanische Künstler persönlich, darunter Kahlo und Rivera, und kaufte Werke direkt von ihnen. Nach Jacques' Tod vermachte Natasha die Sammlung ihrem US-amerikanischen Freund, dem Kurator Robert Littman. Ihr Testament wurde von ihrer Familie erfolglos angefochten. Littman verkaufte die Sammlung 2023 an die in Monterrey ansässige Industriellenfamilie Zambrano. Diese nutzte die Werke anschließend als Sicherheit für einen Kredit der Santander-Bank – so gelangte die Sammlung nach Spanien.

Porträts Natashas spiegeln ihren Wohlstand

Im Faro Santander wird Jacques' Leidenschaft für das Kino anhand zahlreicher Schwarz-Weiß-Fotografien und -Filmstills erzählt. Besonders eindrucksvoll sind die mythisch aufgeladenen Landschaftsaufnahmen und die düsteren urbanen Szenen des gefeierten Kameramanns des Goldenen Zeitalters, Gabriel Figueroa, mit dem Gelman an einigen Filmproduktionen zusammenarbeitete. Zusammen mit Lola Álvarez Bravos fotojournalistischen Einblicken in das städtische Leben und den formalistischen Aufnahmen von Manuel Álvarez Bravo verdeutlichen die Werke die stilistische Vielfalt der modernen mexikanischen Fotografie.

Die Porträts Natashas in der Ausstellung spiegeln den Wohlstand und die Kunstförderung des Ehepaars. Das Bildnis von Kahlo fällt überraschend kühl aus: Es zeigt Gelman als eisige slawische Schönheit, in Pelz gehüllt und mit einem katzenhaften, leicht hochmütigen Ausdruck, der an die Porträts Alberto Giacomettis erinnert. Riveras Porträt – obwohl im selben Jahr entstanden, zeigt es sie schmeichelhaft jünger – stellt Gelman lasziv auf einem Sofa dar. Der Schlitz ihres weißen Kleides gibt den Blick auf ihre langen, wohlgeformten Beine frei. In der Vitrine neben dem Gemälde ist die mit Diamanten besetzte Brosche zu sehen, die Gelman während der Porträtsitzung trug.

Rivera selbst ist die zentrale Figur der Ausstellung. Die gezeigten Werke zeichnen seine künstlerische Entwicklung nach: von frühen kubistischen Arbeiten wie "Last Hour" (1915) bis zu traumartigen Wüstenlandschaften wie "Landscape with Cacti" (1931). Während der späte Rivera vor allem für seine politischen Wandgemälde bekannt war, präsentiert die Ausstellung stattdessen ein kleineres Gemälde: "Sunflowers" (1943). Es zeigt zwei indigene Kinder beim Spielen, von denen eines eine weiße Puppe auseinanderreißt. Das Bild ist unverkennbar didaktisch angelegt, strahlt aber zugleich eine humanistische Wärme aus.

Ein Schwarz-Weiß-Porträt von Richard Silberstein aus dem Jahr 1940 zeigt Rivera und Kahlo in einer Konstellation, in der er beinahe wie eine Vaterfigur wirkt. Riveras Zeichnung einer jungen Kahlo mit entblößten Brüsten ("Nude", 1930) ist dagegen von Sinnlichkeit geprägt. Sie wurde zusammen mit ähnlichen Arbeiten gezeigt: einer eleganten Fotografie eines weiblichen nackten Oberkörpers von Manuel Álvarez Bravo ("Forbidden Fruit", 1970) und einer Zeichnung von José Clemente Orozco, die die üppigen Brüste einer nicht näher bezeichneten Frau zeigt ("Female Nude", undatiert). Im Gegensatz dazu wirken Kahlos Zeichnungen – insbesondere "Abortion" (1932), in der ihr nackter Körper eine anatomische Studie ihrer Organe offenbart, einschließlich einer Nabelschnur, die mit ihrem ungeborenen Kind verbunden ist – durch ihre schonungslose Offenheit verstörend. Sie stellen dem erotischen Mysterium den verletzlichen, von Gewalt geprägten biologischen Körper gegenüber.

Letztlich sind es Kahlos Direktheit und ihr Humor, die die Ausstellung beherrschen. In "Autorretrato (con monos)" (Selbstbildnis mit Affen, 1943) wird ihr strenger Gesichtsausdruck durch vier herumtollende Affen auf spielerische Weise aufgelockert. Einer von ihnen nestelt an der Stickerei ihres Hemdes herum – versucht er, es zu öffnen? Hinter ihrem Rücken blüht eine phallisch anmutende Paradiesvogelblume.

Im Selbstporträt "Diego en mi pensamiento" (Diego in meinen Gedanken, 1943) trägt sie ein traditionelles Tehuana-Kostüm, dessen gestärkte Spitze ihr Gesicht umrahmt. Auf ihre Stirn ist Riveras Gesicht tätowiert. Das Werk wirkt rätselhaft: Die Spitzenfäden winden sich spiralförmig nach außen wie ein Spinnennetz.

Ein noch intimeres Gemälde, "Autorretrato con cama" (Selbstbildnis mit Bett, 1937), zeigt Kahlo sitzend, die Hände im Schoß verschränkt und eine Zigarette haltend. Ihre Haltung ist steif. Die blasse, nackte Puppe auf dem Bett neben ihr wirkt lebensecht und zugleich geisterhaft – ein Verweis auf die Unfruchtbarkeit der Künstlerin.

Ein Höhepunkt ist Kahlos fantastisches Gemälde "El abrazo de amor del universo, la tierra (México), yo, Diego y el señor Xólotl" (Die Liebesumarmung des Universums, der Erde (Mexiko), meiner selbst, Diegos und des Herrn Xólotl, 1949). In einer mondbeschienenen Wüstenlandschaft hält Kahlo den nackten Diego auf ihrem Schoß, wie eine kleine Pietà. Beide sind wiederum in die Arme einer Berggöttin geschmiegt, aus deren Brust Milch fließt. Im Hintergrund erscheint eine weitere göttliche Gestalt, deren Substanz halb aus Erde, halb aus Äther zu bestehen scheint. Das Werk vermittelt den messianischen Eifer, mit dem Rivera und seine Mitstreiter eine moderne, in nationaler Kultur und Mythologie verwurzelte Kunstbewegung schaffen wollten. Indem Kahlo jedoch den wie ein Baby dargestellten Rivera auf ihren Schoß setzt, kehrt sie das Lehrer-Schülerinnen-Verhältnis um, das in einigen ihrer gemeinsamen Porträts zum Ausdruck kommt. Zugleich deutet sie an, dass der größte Mythos, dem sie als wahre Künstlerin verpflichtet war, letztlich ihr eigener war.

Kulturerbe als Kreditsicherheit

Kahlos Starstatus dürfte in den laufenden Rechtsstreitigkeiten in Mexiko eine entscheidende Rolle spielen. Obwohl die Sammlung ursprünglich bis 2030 auf Wanderschaft gehen sollte, fordert das Kollektiv Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Verteidigen wir die Gelman-Sammlung) ihre sofortige Rückgabe. Auch der Oberste Gerichtshof Mexikos wird sich mit dem Fall befassen. Denn ein Präsidialdekret von 1984 verbietet es, "künstlerisches Kulturerbe" außer Landes zu bringen. Der Rechtsstreit verdeutlicht die Risiken, die Banken eingehen, wenn sie kulturelles Erbe verwahren und zugleich wie eine Finanzanlage behandeln.

Die Warnung stammt ausgerechnet von Diego Rivera selbst. In seinem Essay "The Revolutionary Spirit in Modern Art" von 1932 schrieb er, Kunst dürfe niemals zu einer "Art von Börsenware werden, die vom Künstler hergestellt wird", denn sie sei für die Gesellschaft als Ganzes zu wichtig. 90 Jahre später dienen seine Gemälde als Sicherheit für einen Bankkredit. Zugleich hat Mexikos derzeitige linke Regierung zwar versprochen, die Sammlung zurückzuholen, aber drastische Kürzungen im Bereich Kultur und Denkmalschutz vorgenommen. Kritiker sehen deshalb im aktuellen Streit um die Sammlung einen weit größeren politischen Konflikt um Mexikos Vergangenheit und Zukunft.

Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 21, 2026 out of the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Netflix will open the film in New York and Los Angeles on Friday, October 16, then expand wider before coming to Netflix on Friday, December 2.

While it is technically accurate to say that “ La Bola Negra ” is a single feature film from Spain’s beloved creative duo, Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (collective moniker Los Javis ), it feels truer to say that they have made four films and magically contained them within the form of one. It is nearly impossible to grasp the structural effort required to fluidly create one perfectly coherent story using three narratives told across three timelines, each with a distinct visual identity.

“La Bola Negra” comprises a neorealist tale of a closeted young man seeking membership at a casino in 1932, a tragic wartime romance set in 1937, and a lo-fi drama about a historian prompted to investigate all of this in 2017. The fourth element, which serves as the connective tissue for everything, is a timeless poetic expression of love for all the queer storytellers who died before they could truly live .

An unfinished play, “La Bola Negra” by the Spanish poet Federico García Lorca, is the basis of the themes explored across all timelines. Lorca was murdered in 1936 by right-wing militias amid the rising nationalism that led to the Spanish Civil War of 1936-9. In an act of fantastical baton-passing, Los Javis collaborate with Lorca’s spirit to finalize this play, infusing it with details, moods and lyricism from his life and work. Choice lines from his poem “Love Sleeps in the Poet’s Breast” serve as a time-collapsing flash of lightning, reanimating lost souls so that they are briefly, vividly here.

In this reimagined “La Bola Negra,” it is 1932 and 20-year-old Carlos (Milo Quifes) is under pressure from his father to be accepted as a member at their local casino. The meaning of La Bola Negra/ The Black Ball is immediately explicated as roomful of stern homophobic elders vote on his admission with a white ball, meaning “yes” or a black ball meaning “no.” Perhaps you can guess how this vote goes.

Los Javis, aided by sound editors Alejandro Lopez and Anna Harington, use sound design as part of their seamless editing toolkit. The clack, clack, clack of black balls landing plays over the image of an open-topped medical vehicle carrying bodies in 1937. The basis of this second story is “La Piedra Obscura” by Alberto Conejero (2023), a play that re-imagines history to give a different ending to Lorca’s lover, Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, a former Atletico Madrid player who fought and died as a Republican during the 1937 Battle of Santander — the capital of Cantabria (this will be important). Conejero has a screenwriting credit with Los Javis in this queered version of his play.

The 1937 section contains a tortured impossible love story for the ages, while also being the horniest depiction of military life since Claire Denis’ “Beau Travail.” In his first film role, the long-lashed Spanish pop star Guitarricadelafuente plays Sebastián, a young trumpeter whose family is wiped out when Italians bomb his village. Offered the choice between death and Nationalism, he accepts the rifle foisted upon him. When a wounded Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau) is taken as an enemy prisoner in the military hospital, Sebastián’s job is to guard him.

Courageous, principled, tragic, and mind-blowingly hot, Rafael is the platonic ideal of a romantic hero meaning Sebastián, already out of his depth, now also has to deal with an intoxicating crush. His eyes nearly pop out of his head when a nurse tells him to towel off a naked Rafael. The overlapping imagery of sex and violence is never more felt than when Rafael gets so angry that his wound starts bleeding through his bandage.

The real Rafael was described as having a profile like a Greek statue, and Sebastián’s meeting with this flesh-and-blood sculpture is foreshadowed in an extraordinary image from shortly after he loses his family in the bombing. Disoriented and terrified, he runs around until somehow he finds himself crawling up a mound of rubble topped by a fallen statue of Grecian marble. Los Javis express heightened emotions related to love, loss, fear, and regret in compositions that make us pause with the character. Later, in a moment of high anxiety when Rafael is catching a beating, Sebastián will run to the bathroom to play his trumpet (not just a euphemism). Cued by Lorca, Los Javis take poetic license to create magical peaks within a landscape of political realism.

Alberto (Carlos González), the Madrid-based protagonist of the 2017 storyline operates in a more recognizable and grounded sphere. A historian with a particular interest in queer music from 1920s Constantinople, his days are a low-stakes matter of research, casual Grindr user, hanging with his partner Javier (Julio Torres) and handling his explosive mother (Lola Dueñas). The catalyst connecting him to Sebastián, Rafael, Carlos et al. is the news that a grandfather he never met just died and left something especially for him, if only he will travel to Cantabria to collect it. Initially impatient with the whole proposition, Alberto — mirroring the trajectory of Los Javis in making this film — is drawn into a fascinated communion with the history that brought him here.

Each of these three stories is exquisitely crafted on its own individual terms and the triptych becomes dazzling once the subtly seeded internal rhymes begin to set into a cohering fourth underlayer. The screenplay is either perfect or pretty damn close with a refined structure ensuring that every episode on one timeline enhances its neighbors on the others, on both a narrative and thematic level.

Crystalline dialogue sparkles whether it is spoken by a poet, a fascist or Penélope Cruz channeling Drag Queen energy to entertain the Nationalist troops as a Vera Lynn type singer. As the platinum blonde wig-wearing Nene, who comes rolling into a room of roaring soldiers draped sexily on a tank, her sympathies are secretly elsewhere. Sensing something different about Sebastián the moment she sees him amongst her audience, Nene confides in him with lines like, “Transvestism is the fantasy of possibility. War is its opposite.”

Wherever possible, without interrupting the movements of the character and narrative arcs, Los Javis enhance the mood with nods to queer joy and the freedom of expressing the only lifeforce that is truly yours. Music, dance, poetry, and even looking point-blank at the one you desire afford the repressed characters moments of release. The tormented Carlos is briefly himself while dancing flamenco. Sebastián and Rafael transcend their doomed romance through lines of poetry. Who could do otherwise when those lines are, you will never know how much i love you for you sleep within me

Los Javis build out this culturally reverant perspective to honor their partnership with Pedro Almodóvar ( whose fellow competition title “Bitter Christmas” includes a very funny cameo from them) with a fabulous little gag. Meanwhile, Glenn Close shows up in 2017 to play American academic Isabelle Durand, who has dedicated her life to Lorca research and is publishing a volume named “Federica el Poeto Gay.” The gratification of experiencing all the narrative threads coming together is only eclipsed by an awe at the underlying emotional continuity.

All these moving parts are positioned to play like one unbroken piece of music. By the final crescendo, time feels like an illusion and the stories of our dead belong to today.

Grade: A

“La Bola Negra” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
excerpt_original: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi blend real and imaginary people in this Lorca-inspired ode to love stories buried by Spanish history.

article_text:
As James Gunn ‘s fledgling DC Universe continues to grow, he’s revealed that one key character will “almost certainly” return: Harley Quinn. But Margot Robbie , who played the anti-hero in three DCEU movies, may not be back.

On “ The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon? The Official Podcast ,” Gunn was joined by Jennifer Holland and Steve Agee, who starred in his debut DC movie “ The Suicide Squad ,” to discuss which parts of the pre-reboot film will carry over into the new universe. The trio discussed several dead characters from the film and actors that have played multiple DC roles (such as Sean Gunn, Nathan Fillion and Michael Rooker), but ultimately decided that most of the movie is canon to the rebooted DC Universe.

Related Stories

Keanu Reeves' 'Constantine 2' Gets 'Renewed Hope' After James Gunn's DC Exit, Says Director: 'People at DC Were an Impediment to Us'

'Rings of Power' Season 3 Premiere: [SPOILER] Dies in Shocking Murder, Sauron Assembles Ringwraiths and Jamie Campbell Bower Is Galadriel's Lover Celeborn

“That settles it then. I think that ‘The Suicide Squad’ is within the canon of the DCU. It’s decided,” Gunn said. “I’d say, we have one small asterisk, which is what exactly is the future of Harley Quinn? I want to be given a little leeway with this by the fans because I’m not sure exactly how that’s going to manifest itself. But other than that, I think that we can pretty much say the entire movie is canon. I don’t think there’s a problem.”

Earlier in the podcast, Gunn explained that Robbie has become “kind of the biggest female star in the world” and that he isn’t sure if she’d return to play Harley Quinn. She debuted as the first live-action Harley Quinn in David Ayers’ “Suicide Squad” in 2016, then returned for “Birds of Prey” in 2020 before joining Gunn’s standalone sequel in 2021.

“She’s just so crazy. I love her as Harley. I don’t know if she wants to play Harley again. She may be over that,” Gunn said on the podcast. Since “The Suicide Squad,” Robbie has of course conquered the box office as “Barbie” in addition to starring in Emerald Fennell’s “Wuthering Heights.” She’s next set to star in Tim Burton’s “Attack of the Fifty Foot Woman,” so her schedule may be too packed to revist Harley Quinn — at least for now.

Chan）在亚洲的首场个展。展览将画廊转变为一个游戏中心，邀请观众与一组由交互式雕塑和电子游戏组成的新作进行互动。这些新作延续了陈米切尔长期以来的实践，即利用游戏的规则和机制作为社会批判的媒介。这些作品不仅是娱乐，也是陷阱。它们邀请观众以玩家身份参与，但最终将他们锁定在无力劳工的角色中。它们被做过手脚的机制剥夺了使用者的自主性，反而要求不间断的工作，暴露了晚期资本主义劳动无可逃脱的循环。这些与其说是隐喻，不如说是对一个完全按预期运作的系统的切实演示，展示了如何让劳动感觉像游戏一样，反而会巩固这种劳动的结构，而不是提供逃离它的途径。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览呈现了六件独特的交互式雕塑作品，它们由机电弹珠机组件和定制的电子游戏图形管线构建而成。每一件都是一个色彩缤纷的微型场景箱，描绘了不同的工作世界：办公室、工厂、农场、家庭、直播、交易大厅，邀请参观者拿起弹球拨片。去玩吧，你会发现它们被动了手脚：技巧只是一种幻觉，险过也是被精心设计出来的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "中心是一款电子游戏，用令人满足的分数、动作和声音来抚慰玩家。随着游戏的进行，玩家意识到游戏场地并非为他们自己的享受而建造；他们的输入汇入了一个更大的自治系统。这些机制与其说是隐喻，不如说是对一个完全按预期运作的系统的切实演示，展示了如何让劳动感觉像游戏一样，反而会巩固结构而不是提供逃离的途径。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/stratus.campaign-image.com/images/746661000026309003_zc_v6_1679290775033_desarthelogo.jpg?w=840&ssl=1", "alt": "https://zohopublic.com/zohocampaigns/746661000026309003_zc_v10_1678758926086_blindspot_gallery_logo_fi.jpg", "caption": "", "credit": "Artomity", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Mitchell F. Chan / Workers’ Playtime / Oct 10 – Nov 21, 2026 / Opening: Saturday, Oct 10, 3pm – 7pm / Artist-guided tour led by Mitchell F. Chan starts at 5pm /

DE SARTHE 2/F, Block A, Vita Tower 29 Wong Chuk Hang Road, Hong Kong +852 2167 8896 Tuesday – Saturday, 11am – 7pm

desarthe.com

DE SARTHE is pleased to present Workers’ Playtime , the first solo exhibition in Asia by Toronto-based conceptual digital media artist Mitchell F. Chan. The exhibition transforms the gallery into a game center, inviting viewers to interact with a new body of work consisting of interactive sculptures and video games. These new pieces extend Chan’s ongoing practice of using the rules and mechanics of games as a medium for social critique. These works are more than just entertainment; they are also traps. They invite viewers to engage as players, but ultimately lock them into roles as ineffectual laborers. Their rigged mechanisms deny the user’s agency and instead demand relentless work, exposing the inescapable loop of late capitalist labor. These are not metaphors so much as working demonstrations of a system functioning exactly as intended, of how making labor feel like play can reinforce the structure of that labor rather than offer an escape from it.

The exhibition features six distinct interactive sculptural works built from electromechanical pinball components and custom video game graphics pipelines. Each a colorful shadowbox depicting a different world of work: the office, the factory, the farm, the home, the livestream, the trading floor, invite visitors to take the flippers. Play them and you will find they are rigged: the skill is an illusion, the near-miss engineered.

At the center is a video game that soothes the player with a satisfying wash of points, motion and sound. As the game progresses, the player realizes that the playfield is not build for their own enjoyment; their inputs feed into a larger, autonomous system. These mechanisms are not metaphors so much as working demonstrations of a system functioning exactly as intended, of how making labor feel like play can reinforce the structure rather than offer an escape from it.

的长期项目；以及她从乌克兰拍摄的肖像——出自她2024年由 GOST 出版的新书《此地与彼地：一次某种形式的远征》（Here and There: An Expedition of Sorts）。埃德尔斯坦还创作过关于男性自杀、移民、约旦河西岸以及英国贫困问题的作品，并曾为《纽约时报杂志》、《金融时报周末杂志》、《Vogue》、《GQ》和《Esquire》等刊物拍摄肖像。英国国家肖像馆（National Portrait Gallery）收藏了她超过100幅摄影原作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Offenders），在那里她主要与身处监狱或刚被释放的男性打交道。这项工作充满了活力与同情心，但她在大学期间发现了摄影，并很快决定拍摄纪实和肖像影像是一种延续社会工作的方式，“而不必写出案件报告”，她说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她在工作日担任助手，这使她得以学习技术技巧以及如何使用灯光和冲印，并在南非人们为推翻种族隔离而抗争、社会动荡不安的时期，开始担任新闻摄影师。最终她成为了一名全职新闻摄影记者，于1982–83年为《兰德每日邮报》（The Rand Daily Mail）工作，并于1984年为《明星报》（The Star）工作。她与黑人同事并肩作战，并且深知自己相比他们的特权，她说；作为一个白人，她能够承受更大的风险，“因为对他们而言代价要高得多，他们必须循规蹈矩”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "埃德尔斯坦的工作曾获奖项，但在1985年，她决定离开，前往伦敦印刷学院（London College of "text": "不过，埃德尔斯坦表示，她很感激自己当时能成为一名新闻摄影师，当时的报社还保留着全职岗位，约稿也更加丰厚；她能靠这份工作养活自己，这些约稿也帮助她更容易接触到那些难以接近的人物。她的许多个人项目都包含委任创作的元素，例如《真相与谎言》中对纳尔逊·曼德拉的拍摄，或者《亲密关系》中对喜剧演员法兰奇与桑德斯（French and Saunders）的拍摄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但她的成功并非仅仅归功于运气或当时的体制；在一个极度由男性主导的环境中——且作为单亲母亲——她依然努力利用自己的工作去帮助他人。事实上，她对权力和强加的不公有着敏锐的察觉。“回看这些照片，我惊叹于自己的作品在多大程度上受到了我早期对不平等和征服的经历或互动的影响，”她在斯蒂尔斯的展览资料中写道，“一方对另一方施加了不公正的优越感。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Now extended until the end of October, Jillian Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery, Edinburgh shows her deep engagement with people, from those at South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation to swimmers at Hampstead Heath

Born in Cape Town, Jillian Edelstein is best-known for her work on South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Photographing perpetrators, victims, and other individuals involved in the public hearings which grappled with the country’s Apartheid history from 1996-2002 – and some of the landscapes involved – Edelstein worked on the project for four years. When she published it as a book in 2002, Truth and Lies included endorsements from Archbishop Desmond Tutu, Gillian Slovo and Pumla Gobodo-Madikizela (Research Chair in Studies in Historical Trauma and Transformation at Stellenbosch University in South Africa), plus extensive text and reflections written by Edelstein.

But though Truth and Lies is important, it’s also not the only thing Edelstein has made. In fact when she made it she wasn’t living in South Africa any more; she has now been a UK resident for much longer than she lived in Africa. Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery includes Truth and Lies , but it also includes other projects from across her five decades of work. Curated by Tracey Marshall-Grant, it’s titled Jillian Edelstein – Among People to mark the photographer’s commitment to individuals from many different communities, and includes early images from Johannesburg and Cape Town, and from an anthropological project in Portugal, right up to recent work from 2020-22, showing the community of swimmers who use Hampstead Heath’s ponds.

“ People are people and you can learn from everyone. I try to treat everyone with equality.” Jillian Edelstein

It also includes images from Edelstein’s long-running portrait series Affinities , which explores creative partnerships; her long term project on the Sangoma, traditional healers on the Lesotho-South African border; and portraits taken from Ukraine, from her book Here and There: An Expedition of Sorts , published by GOST in 2024. Edelstein has also made work about male suicide, migration, the West Bank, and poverty in the UK, and has shot portraits for publications such as The New York Times Magazine, The FT Weekend Magazine, Vogue, GQ, and Esquire . The National Portrait Gallery holds more than 100 of her prints.

She has shot people from wildly different communities and walks of life, in fact, from those immersed in wealth to those facing very hard times. “It’s a privilege, because people are people and you can learn from everyone,” says Edelstein. “I try to treat everyone with equality, I think that can show something really powerful…In South Africa I remember thinking how fascinating it was that the perpetrators put themselves forward to be captured, in a vain kind of way. That was very striking. I think there is quantifiable experience, and you have to face that and think how to portray it.”

Born in 1958, Edelstein originally studied social work rather than photography; her first job was at the National Institute for the Crime and Rehabilitation of Offenders in Cape Town, where she worked with mainly men who were in prison, or had recently been released. There was energy and compassion in this work, but she had discovered photography at university and soon decided that shooting documentary and portrait images was a way to continue social work “without having to write out the case report”, she says.

Working as an assistant during the week, which allowed her to learn technical skills as well as how to use lights and print, she started to work as a press photographer at a time of great unrest in South Africa, as people struggled to overthrow Apartheid. Eventually she became a photojournalist, working for The Rand Daily Mail in 1982–83, and The Star newspaper in 1984. She worked alongside Black colleagues and was well aware of her privilege compared to them, she says; she was able to take greater risks as a White, “because the costs for them would have been so much higher, they had to keep in line”.

Edelstein won awards for her work but in 1985 decided to leave to formally study documentary photography at the London College of Printing [now the London College of Communication]. She lasted six months before Michael Cranmer, then-picture editor of The Sunday Times , came to do a guest lecture and saw some of her work. “He said ‘What are you doing here?!’” Edelstein laughs. “He gave me a commission and then Andrew Neil [then-editor of The Sunday Times ] saw the portrait and said ‘Offer her a contract’. It was sort of extraordinary even then.”

Edelstein says she is grateful to have been a press photographer then though, when staff jobs did exist and commissions were more generous; she could support herself with this work, and the commissions also helped her access to hard-to-reach individuals. Many of her personal projects include commissioned elements, such as the portrait of Nelson Mandela in Truth and Lies , or the comedians French and Saunders in Affinities.

But her success also wasn’t just down to luck or the structures of the day; working in an extremely male-dominated environment – and as a single mother – she still tried to leverage her work to help others. In fact she’s acutely aware of power, and how it’s unfairly brought to bear. “Looking back across these photographs, I’m struck by how much my work has been shaped by my early engagements or interactions with inequality and subjugation,” she states in Stills’ press material, “one asserting an unjust superiority over another”.

She tells me that her training in social work, anthropology, psychology and sociology helped her refine these insights; she thinks about power at both a macro and micro level, in terms of the interpersonal and the societal. There’s the delicate balance between directing a shoot and giving her subjects space, for example, but then there’s also authority and how it plays out. She tells me an anecdote about photographing five members of the security police in South Africa, for example, who were testifying before the Truth Commission for the murder of one of their Black colleagues, who they had decided was informing on them to the ANC; it was a difficult, intimidating shoot but a few days later she saw one of the men on his own in the airport, lacking all the bravado of his strength-in-numbers.

Edelstein is also well-attuned to the role of photography and observation, however, the negative ways in which the gaze can be used, and she can therefore be implicated. In Truth and Lies she writes about the bright lights which illuminated the townships in the 1970s and 80s, the ‘eye of the state’ which kept residents under surveillance. In the West Bank she noted something similar in the turnstiles, she says, which allows Israeli soldiers to control peoples’ movements. “This practical handiwork that autocratic governments put in place, it operates and it’s horrifying,” she says.

Edelstein is also saddened by the current state of the world, the fact that terrible things happen and that “no matter how present the camera is, it hasn’t stopped them”. Even so, she’s still enthusiastic about her current work, which includes a commission photographing women who have survived sexual violence and abuse. “It’s the challenge of photographing someone, the dance that you have to do,” she says. “What you give is what you get back.” Then she smiles and asks me about myself.

Jillian Edelstein – Among People is on show at Stills until 31 October https://stills.org/exhibitions/exhibition-jillian-edelstein/

article_text:
A fter a windy road, this week it finally happened . The day that Hollywood, and many of those who are invested in it, had been dreading, the grimly inevitable disappearance of Warner Bros as it was consumed by what is now known as Paramount. The two once-classic studios will become one – Skydance, the David Ellison-owned company that has infinitely more money than common sense or base-level creativity.

The week has seen many, including the Guardian , speculate about what we may be able to expect, what kind of films the billion-dollar behemoth might now be releasing. Warners after all has created classics such as Casablanca, The Exorcist and 2001: A Space Odyssey while Paramount has been behind The Godfather, Chinatown and Breakfast at Tiffany’s. Just imagine what the combined might of these two prestigious, industry-defining studios could achieve with the promise of 30-plus theatrical releases a year, huge amounts of money and considerable manpower at play.

Arriving just days after the deal was made official, Skydance’s Matchbox: the Movie suggests that the future is even bleaker than we had anticipated.

Like most of the company’s previous films, it’s an empty-headed, synthetically made action film cobbled together as if by machinery only, so lacking in personality or even vigour that it’s impossible to believe anyone involved was there for anything but an undeserved paycheck. It’s a two-hour Apple TV film based on the Matchbox toy vehicle line, a sentence no one should have had to hear in this lifetime, and it’s exactly as disposable and dead-eyed as that would imply.

How would that film make any sense, one might ask, and well it doesn’t, the toy awkwardly used as a way to bond a group of young friends in the 90s before leaping forward to present day as they reunite. One of them ( John Cena ) has become a super spy and after he returns home for a funeral, he accidentally involves his childhood gang (Jessica Biel, Sam Richardson, Teyonah Parris and Arturo Castro playing gay – LGBTQ+ representation in a Matchbox movie, we did it!) in a mission to save a nuclear warhead. Cue antics and vehicles and lines like “Maybe I need to think inside the box” as if a Mattel exec was on set insisting on as many nods as humanly possible.

The action comedy has become the most depressingly common, and most reliably awful, streaming genre and Matchbox, despite whatever loosely defined IP it’s attached to, might not be the worst but it’s among the most aggressively anonymous. The worst remains Apple’s Chris Evans-Ana de Armas multi-vehicle pile-up Ghosted (another Skydance classic!) but that film’s awfulness and utter incompetence did at least make it drunkenly entertaining, a satisfyingly punchable piñata. There’s no joy to be had in ribbing this one, it’s more competently made (by Sam Hargrave, a stuntman turned director of the Extraction franchise) but it’s just so devoid of colour, its stench the result of total no-tries blandness (thanks to a script from David Coggeshall, whose credits include hokey horrors The Deliverance and Orphan: First Kill).

Dialogue feels consistently, boringly AI-generated throughout and while textured characters would have been unfair to expect here, it’s not a stretch to hope for some mild laughs along the way. But the comedy is of the predictably smug and quippy variety, the kind of film where a character is mid-action telling someone on the phone that they’re “a little busy right now”. The pairing of a slick super agent with regular civilians is also so exhaustingly overdone at this stage and despite what could have maybe been a slightly more interesting angle – young friends transplanting a playground dynamic to a globe-hopping, bomb-exploding action stage – it’s just more of the “woah, he just did that!” bumbling that even the cast seem bored with. A plasticky, unenthused Cena is stuck in autopilot once again (I think that button might actually be broken) while a similarly flat Biel, bizarrely choosing this as her first film in almost a decade, makes zero effort to convincingly play anyone but herself, styled up as if she walked to set from home (a petrol-stained small town ambulance-driving car enthusiast she is not).

I wasn’t a big fan of Greta Gerwig’s overpraised Barbie but it was at least a respectably large swing, a smart enough justification for why Mattel might actually need a Hollywood arm. But this is exactly what we should more reasonably anticipate from their output (Jon M Chu’s Hot Wheels and Vin Diesel’s Rock ’Em Sock ’Em Robots are both on the way). No one needed a Matchbox movie that dissected toxic masculinity or used toy cars as a metaphor for anything, but no one really needed a Matchbox movie in the first place. As boredom swept over me during the film’s truly punishing runtime, I imagined better ways to mash the words Matchbox and movie together. I came to the natural conclusion that doing so would be obviously ungodly but even my worst idea was better than “what if another sloppy streaming action comedy but with Matchbox mentions?” Ellison and Skydance have amassed a great deal of power and capital in Hollywood but junk like this is a glum warning sign of what will be done with it.

Matchbox: the Movie is out on Apple TV+ on 9 October

article_text:
A24’s “ You Can See Everything ” narrowly beat Warner Bros. and DC’s “ Clayface ” at the Friday box office, cementing its status as the must-watch documentary — or film, for that matter — of the moment.

The buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc generated $3.56 million on its third Friday from an expanded 3,243 North American theaters and should earn $10.65 million by Sunday, per rival estimates. That’s on top of the cumulative $56.85 million it’s already pulled in across North America since it opened in theaters on Oct. 16.

Related Stories

'Dune 3' Popcorn Bucket Has Two Sandworms That 'Make It Easier to Share'

Zendaya Sets ‘Dune 3’ Oscar Campaign for Best Actress in Category Shake-Up (EXCLUSIVE)

Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

Just behind the doc, “Clayface” landed at No. 2 on its second Friday, making $3.3 million from 3,478 North American theaters. The gory DC film has made $36.9 million domestically so far, with rival estimates suggesting the film will gross another $10.25 million by Sunday.

Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star. Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.”

Laika’s “ Wildwood ” landed in third place on Friday, grossing $2.39 million from 3,100 North American theaters. Featuring a voice cast that includes Carey Mulligan, Jacob Tremblay and others, the stop-motion film looks to add another $7 to $8 million to its cumulative domestic gross of $25.2 million through its second weekend in theaters.

Directed by Travis Knight, “Wildwood” revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted. Strong reviews should continue to propel the lavish film at the box office, which carries a substantial $100 million price tag.

Black Bear’s “ Wicker ” followed with $1.43 million in its second Friday from 2,374 North American theaters, landing in fifth place behind the concert film “BTS World Tour ‘ARIRANG’ in South America,” which brought in $2 million from 1,010 North American theaters. Described as an “audacious comedic fable,” “Wicker” is targeting another $4.1 million in its sophomore weekend, adding to its $13 million cumulative domestic gross.

“Wicker” tells the love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband (Alexander Skarsgård) from the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Elizabeth Debicki also stars.

title_original: From a VR gay sauna to the gothic pile that inspired Cluedo – Fierce festival storms back
editorial_title_zh: 从VR同性恋桑拿到启发《妙探寻凶》的哥特宅邸——Fierce艺术节强势回归
editorial_excerpt_zh: 伯明翰多个场地 随着英国历史最悠久的现场艺术节回归，准备好迎接深夜艺术家晚宴、一场在游泳池中的演出，以及费伊·德里斯科尔令人惊叹的旋转式崩解。“两件事可以同时为真”这句话在通俗心理学中频繁出现……

"“两件事可以同时为真”这句话在通俗心理学中频繁出现，我发现，它也是人们在目睹现场艺术中那些走得更远的作品时经常给出的回应。嗯，这场表演究竟是令人困惑的自我沉溺，还是彻底深刻？有时两者兼有。事实上，可以同时为真的不止两件事，而是观众中有多少人就有多少件事，因为这一切都关乎此刻的现场主观体验；在场与连接。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fierce创办于1998年，是英国历史最悠久的现场艺术节。在一周时间里，它接管伯明翰的常规剧院以及非传统空间，尤其是正在迅速成为创意中心的旧工业区迪格贝斯。今年的节目还包括：深夜艺术家晚宴、一场在游泳池中的演出，以及在一座宏伟哥特式大厅里举行的六小时表演即兴聚会——据说那座大厅正是《妙探寻凶》的灵感来源。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "重点在于感官与感知；一切都关乎身体。但我体验的第一件作品实际上是在虚拟现实中：台湾艺术家周东彦的《Traversing the Mist》。场景设定在一间同性恋桑拿，VR技术令人印象深刻。你走过灰色混凝土走廊、更衣室、淋浴间、小隔间，推开你明知并不真正存在的帘子。你可以开门、捡起东西、按电梯按钮。你是这个诡异场景的观察者，场景中满是面容空白、彼此相同的男人；一种寻觅之感弥漫其间，却找不到丝毫喜悦或快感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d3b1678470e53750586d1d1694467c244575f2cb/0_0_5941_3961/master/5941.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "两个身影在发光的雾气中呈现剪影，似乎正俯身亲吻", "caption": "缺乏连接……周东彦，《In the Mist》，Fierce艺术节，2026年。摄影：Kris Kang", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种体验兼具沉浸与疏离。它引人投入，却又诡异孤独——当地面塌陷、扰乱你自己的本体感觉时，也令人不安。你有所感受，但你感受到的恰恰是缺乏连接。（周东彦还展出了一部坐着观看的短片VR作品《In the Mist》，它是那部长篇作品的前身，但基本上就是一部悲伤的色情片。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "VR中缺失的是气味、热度、汗水。但别担心，别处多的是。沃伊切赫·格鲁津斯基汗湿、多毛、过于人性的肉身，在他的独舞《Threesome》中处于正前方与中心；他穿着无底荷叶边内裤，在肩倒立中做倒置的普利耶，以及其他瑜伽动作，屁股朝天。在画外音中，他向我们讲述三位因同性恋身份而蒙羞的波兰芭蕾舞者，而《Threesome》正是他试图夺回他们真实身份、并与自己“可怖”的身体和解的尝试。一连串露臀的扭曲动作，接着是一段狂欢式、重复的吉格舞，是做到这一点的最佳方式吗？嗯，这是格鲁津斯基的方式。而且它奇怪地引人入胜，逐渐推向某种宣泄，伴随着灯光、音乐和挑衅的情绪。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术家Melissandre Varin以n:u为名，自称“氛围制造者”，这是个有趣的品牌定位，或许会改变观众的期待。Fierce是一个彻底国际化的艺术节，但n:u此前常驻伯明翰，尽管其作品根植于刚果、瓜德罗普和贝宁传统。我赶上了作品《FREE(HOLD)》排练的一部分，那是一场晦涩的仪式，表演者拖着绳索绕在脚踝上，向天空哀号。忍耐、苦难、奴隶制和殖民主义一齐涌上心头。", "translated": true}, "text": "这是一个充满引人入胜、能开启对话的作品的艺术节，但美国编舞家费伊·德里斯科尔以她备受赞誉、获奖的作品《Weathering》把其他所有人都远远甩在后面，该作在此进行英国首演。德里斯科尔的作品在概念、投入、执行和规模上都高出几个层级。它本质上是10位表演者在一个旋转平台上，一幅活人画，或者与其说是活人画，不如说是一幅在生活压力或仅仅是时间流逝的重力下缓慢扭曲、衰败、塌陷的画面。", article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "T he phrase “two things can be true” is a frequent refrain in popular psychology and it’s also a frequent response, I find, to witnessing the farther reaches of live art. Hmm, is this performance confusingly self-indulgent or utterly profound? Sometimes it can be both. In fact, it’s not just two things that can be true, it’s as many things as there are people in the audience, since this is all about the live subjective experience, in the moment; presence and connection."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Launched in 1998, Fierce is Britain’s longest-running live art festival. For one week it takes over Birmingham’s conventional theatres alongside unconventional spaces, especially in ex-industrial Digbeth, which is fast becoming a creative hub. Also on the bill this year: late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool, and a six-hour performance jam at a grand gothic hall that was apparently the inspiration for Cluedo."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There’s a focus on the sensuous and sensory; it’s all about the physical body. But the first piece I experience is actually in virtual reality: Traversing the Mist, by Taiwanese artist Tung-Yen Chou. The setting is a gay sauna, and the VR tech is impressive. You walk through the grey concrete corridors, locker room, showers, cubicles, pushing aside curtains that you know aren’t really there. You can open doors, pick things up, press buttons in the lift. You’re an observer of the uncanny scene, which is peopled by identical blank-faced men; a sense of searching pervades, but there’s zero joy or pleasure to be found."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d3b1678470e53750586d1d1694467c244575f2cb/0_0_5941_3961/master/5941.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Two figures are silhouetted against lit mist as they appear to lean in for a kiss", "caption": "Lack of connection … Tung-Yen Chou, In the Mist at Fierce festival, 2026. article_text:
T he phrase “two things can be true” is a frequent refrain in popular psychology and it’s also a frequent response, I find, to witnessing the farther reaches of live art. Hmm, is this performance confusingly self-indulgent or utterly profound? Sometimes it can be both. In fact, it’s not just two things that can be true, it’s as many things as there are people in the audience, since this is all about the live subjective experience, in the moment; presence and connection.

Launched in 1998, Fierce is Britain’s longest-running live art festival. For one week it takes over Birmingham’s conventional theatres alongside unconventional spaces, especially in ex-industrial Digbeth, which is fast becoming a creative hub. Also on the bill this year: late-night artist dinners, a show in a swimming pool, and a six-hour performance jam at a grand gothic hall that was apparently the inspiration for Cluedo.

There’s a focus on the sensuous and sensory; it’s all about the physical body. But the first piece I experience is actually in virtual reality: Traversing the Mist, by Taiwanese artist Tung-Yen Chou. The setting is a gay sauna, and the VR tech is impressive. You walk through the grey concrete corridors, locker room, showers, cubicles, pushing aside curtains that you know aren’t really there. You can open doors, pick things up, press buttons in the lift. You’re an observer of the uncanny scene, which is peopled by identical blank-faced men; a sense of searching pervades, but there’s zero joy or pleasure to be found.

The experience is a combination of immersive and detached. It’s engaging, and yet eerily lonely – and also unnerving when the floor falls away, messing with your own proprioception. You feel, but what you feel is exactly the lack of connection. (Chou is also showing a short, sit-down VR piece called In the Mist, which was a precursor to the longer work, but is basically a sad porno.)

What you’re missing in VR is the smells, the heat, the sweat. But don’t worry, there’s plenty of that elsewhere. Wojciech Grudziński’s sweaty, hairy, all-too-human fleshy body is front and centre in his solo Threesome, his bum in the air as he does upside down pliés in a shoulder stand and other yogic moves wearing bottomless frilly knickers. In voiceover he tells us of three Polish ballet dancers who were shamed for their homosexuality, and Threesome is his attempt to reclaim their true identities, and make peace with his own “ghastly” body. Is a series of bum-bearing contortions followed by a ravey, repetitive jig the best way to do that? Well, it’s Grudziński’s way. And it’s strangely compelling, building to a sort of catharsis, with lights and music and defiant mood.

Artist Melissandre Varin is known as n:u, and calls themself an “atmosphere-maker”, which is interesting branding and perhaps modifies the expectations of the audience. Fierce is a thoroughly international festival, but n:u was previously based in Birmingham, although the work is rooted in Congolese, Guadeloupean, and Beninese heritage. I caught part of a rehearsal for the piece FREE(HOLD), an opaque ritual, in which performers drag ropes around their ankles and keen to the sky. Endurance, suffering, slavery and colonialism all rushed to mind.

This is a festival full of intriguing, conversation-starting stuff, but American choreographer Faye Driscoll blows everyone else out of the water with her acclaimed, award-winning piece Weathering, which gets its UK premiere here. Driscoll’s work is a few levels up in terms of concept, commitment, execution and scale. It’s essentially 10 performers on a rotating platform, a tableau vivant, or maybe less a living tableau than one that’s slowly distorting and decaying and caving under the gravity of life’s pressures, or just the passage of time.

article_text:
In advance of its first-ever regular season game in Paris on Sunday, the National Football League announced NFL Color Field—“a new platform that brings football and visual arts together through large-scale installations, original programming and immersive cultural experiences,” as a press release describes it.

Over the coming weekend, a painting by Jammie Holmes will figure in hand-painted end zones created for a flag-football field that will be set up beneath the Eiffel Tower as part of an NFL Experience Paris installation. A Louisiana native and recent fellow at Paris’s Académie des beaux-arts and Cité internationale des arts, Holmes is a fan of the New Orleans Saints, who will play the Pittsburgh Steelers in the City of Light.

The new initiative is an off-shoot of NFL Artist Replay, a program launched in 2023 “to spotlight diverse artistic voices and celebrate the stories, identities, and cultural perspectives that shape the world of football.” In Paris and also in another iteration planned for Miami Art Week in December, NFL Color Field—curated by Jasmine Martin of Pivotal Arts—“builds on that foundation, anchoring each moment with a signature artist partnership and large-scale installation that transforms a football field into a canvas for original artwork.”

Holmes, who recently discovered that his great-grandfather was stationed in France and visited Montmartre during World War I, said, “There’s something powerful about bringing a piece of Louisiana and Saints fandom to Paris, especially knowing that my own family’s history stretches across both places. So much of my art is about the things we carry with us, like our memories, our families and our backgrounds.” He continued: “I hope it shows young people that creativity is possible for them too—that they can take their own stories and roots and turn them into something that reaches the world.”
excerpt_original: A painting by Jammie Holmes will feature in a flag-football field installed beneath the Eiffel Tower.

article_text:
We’re thrilled to announce that Factory 25, the celebrated Brooklyn-based independent film distribution company, has acquired world rights on Jaclyn Bethany’s acclaimed drama In Transit , starring Alex Sarrigeorgiou (who also wrote the script), François Arnaud ( Heated Rivalry) , and Jennifer Ehle. Winner of the Audience Award for Best Narrative Feature at NewFest, Factory 25 will give the film a theatrical release beginning November 1 and a digital debut on December 1. Ahead of the roll-out, we’re pleased to debut the exclusive trailer and poster.

Here’s the synopsis: “In a small town in Maine, Lucy tends bar at the local dive where she’s worked for years, content in the rhythms of her quiet life with her longtime boyfriend, Tom. But when Ilse, a mysterious older artist adrift in her own life, asks Lucy to model for her, each woman stirs in the other the possibility of a different kind of meaning. Just as Lucy learns the bar is being sold and the life she’s built may be slipping away, she has to reckon with what she truly wants.”

One of the themes that interests me most as a filmmaker is intimacy between women,” said Jaclyn Bethany. “It is quite simply something we do not see enough on screen. When I received the script for In Transit I was instantly transported to Lucy and Ilse’s world — two women from completely different backgrounds who are brought together by fate, art and desire. Alex’s script is beautiful, subtle and thought provoking. I knew I wanted to direct this film. The film presents a study of a relationship that we may have seen before, (an artist and muse) but subsequently turns this relationship on its head. With a poetic approach and artistic lens, every frame is carefully chosen, every word precisely spoken. In Transit explores a unique and invigorating relationship between two women, exploring many aspects of femininity, female sexuality and the vulnerability of womanhood – both through our bodies and minds. The film is a chamber piece, rotating solely around two strong women and their desires. I believe most women can see aspects of themselves through each character.”

See the exclusive trailer and poster below.

article_text:
14年ぶりの「オネーギン」公演

東京バレエ団の「オネーギン」公演（11月6日～、新国立劇場）を前に、都内で公開リハーサルが行われました。 映画「ジョン・クランコ バレエの革命児」で、再び脚光を浴びた天才振付家ジョン・クランコ（1927—1973）の代表作とされる「オネーギン」に、同団として14年ぶりに挑戦します。

この日は振付指導の ジェーン・ボーン氏や、以前の公演で主役を務めた斎藤友佳理団長らのアドバイスを受けながら、チャイコフスキーの抒情的な旋律に乗せてオネーギン役の宮川新大さん、タチヤーナ役の沖香菜子さん、秋山瑛さんらがパ・ド・ドゥの場面などを披露しました。

ロシアの文豪、アレクサンドル・プーシキンの名作「 エヴゲーニイ・オネーギン 」に基づく物語は1820年代のロシアが舞台。誠実なタチヤーナと憂鬱な貴公子オネーギンの悲劇的な恋の行方が、ドラマティックに描かれます。「 鏡のパ・ド・ドゥ」や「手紙のパ・ド・ドゥ」で特に知られる クランコの振付は流麗でかつ非常に技巧的で、手足が複雑に絡み合う場面も多く、キャストは何度も動きを確認しながら、入念にリハーサルを進めていました。

クランコの振付で感情をいかに表現するか

リハーサル後、取材に応じたキャストは様々な表現でクランコの緻密な振付の魅力と難しさについて触れました。

オネーギン役の柄本弾さんは「まず技術面をクリアすることが感情表現へのステップ。田舎の空気に馴染めないオネーギンの感情などをいかに表すかを考えています」と語り、宮川新大さんは「 クラシックとは異なる重心やパートナーとの組み方に苦心しつつ、毎日のリハーサルで新しい学びを得ています 」と話していました。

沖香菜子さんは「 正確な振付・カウントを守りつつ、機械的にならないよう自分に落とし込み、迷いなく踊る状態を目指しています。あらためて、 演技に集中するためには基礎の徹底が不可欠と感じました 」とコメント。秋山瑛さんは「 クランコの振付は感情を伝える『言語』。基礎がなければ溢れる感情を表現しきれないです。 数センチの角度やラインなど微細なディテールへのこだわりが作品の質を決定づけると思います」と話していました。

注目の公演は11月6日～8日で4公演が行われます。東京・初台の新国立劇場。公演情報やチケットについては（ https://thetokyoballet.com/performance/onegin2026/ ）へ。

（美術展ナビ編集班 岡部匡志）

article_text:
Te puede interesar

Netflix anunció una nueva serie de Stranger Things: de qué tratará Otros Mundos y cuándo se estrenará

Qué ver este fin de semana en streaming: cinco producciones imperdibles de Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, HBO Max y Apple TV

El thriller argentino inspirado en hechos reales estrenará sus siete episodios el 18 de noviembre y retratará la historia de Aníbal Gordon, un criminal vinculado a la violencia paraestatal de los años 70.

Netflix presentó el tráiler oficial de Gordon , la nueva serie argentina protagonizada por Rodrigo de la Serna que llegará a la plataforma el próximo 18 de noviembre . Dirigida por Pablo Trapero y Pablo Fendrik , la ficción de siete episodios reconstruye la historia de Aníbal Gordon, un delincuente que se involucró en la violencia paraestatal durante los años 70 en Argentina.

Basada en las novelas Gordon y Gordon, el aniquilador , de Marcelo Larraquy, la producción cuenta con un elenco integrado por Matías Recalt, Camila Peralta, Fiorella Bottaioli, Agustín Pardella, Fernando Contigiani y Agustina Muñoz , además de la participación especial de Matías Mayer.

La serie está producida por Adrián Suar y Diego Andrasnik, de Preludio Producciones, y fue filmada en distintas localidades de Buenos Aires y en Bariloche. Según Trapero, la ficción busca ofrecer una mirada sobre un período histórico y un personaje que invite a la reflexión más allá del último episodio.

¿De qué va?

Inspirada en hechos reales, la serie sigue la transformación de Aníbal Gordon, un delincuente común que, sin abandonar sus actividades criminales, se convirtió en un implacable agente paraestatal en el contexto de la violencia política argentina de la década de 1970.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Prime Video has named former Netflix Germany film chief Sasha Bühler as Philip Pratt ‘s successor at the Amazon streamer.

Bühler has been named Head of German Originals at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios Germany, news that comes months after we revealed she had left her role as Director of Film for German-speaking Europe at Netflix. She will begin on December 1.

The role puts her in charge of a slate that includes YA mega-hit Maxton Hall – The World Between Us, The Tank and the local version of LOL: Last One Laughing. She will be responsible for development, commissioning and launches of upcoming Prime Video titles such as Superior , Holey Moley – Minigolf Extreme , Der erste letzte Tag and The Prototype.

Related Stories

Amazon MGM Studios Japan To Double Investment In Original Content; 'One Piece' & 'Kingdom' Producers Talk IP Strategies - TIFFCOM

Casting Round-Up: Arthur McAlpine III To Recur On Starz Black Rodeo Drama; Gillian Nation Joins 'Baywatch' & Desmin Borges Cast In 'Rose Hill'

She replaces Philip Pratt, who earlier this month was named VP, Original Production at Disney+ Germany, Switzerland and Austria to oversee commissioning in the region. He is effectively replacing the exiting Benjamina Mirnik-Voges.

Watch on Deadline

Bühler will report into Tara Erer, Director of Northern European Originals, UK Unscripted & Film, who in turn works within Nicole Clemens’ UK and international originals team at Amazon MGM Studios.

The hire is big news in Germany, where the global streamers are increasingly focused on original programming and building subscription numbers. With exec changes at Disney, Netflix and Amazon in recent months, producers will be eager to see what this means for their prospects.

At Netflix, Bühler made a reputation as a key gatekeeper in the local film market, and was behind the streamer’s involvement in the Oscar-winning war movie All Quiet on the Western Front . Her credits also counted Blood Red Sky and Army of Thieves , and more recent pics such as Exterritorial and Brick, both of which are among Netflix’s all-time top ten non-English language films, on her credits.

Jan Bennemann has replaced her as Head of Film for Germany, Austria and Switzerland at Netflix.

Further back in her career, Bühler spent more than a decade at Constantin Film as Head of Acquisitions and International Co-Productions and was Head of Acquisitions at SquareOne Entertainment.

In an internal note seen by Deadline, Erer wrote: “Sasha brings exceptionally strong relationships with filmmakers, actors and producers in Germany and has a reputation that precedes her. She is smart, decisive, optimistic and very ambitious in the stories she wants to tell, and understands both local and global audiences.

“Her arrival is a real statement of our growth and ambition in the region. As we scale German originals, Sasha is exactly the kind of leader to help us reach for bigger and bolder stories. Simply, she is brilliant and a rare find, so I’m thrilled that she is coming over to join our fantastic Northern Europe team.

article_text:
Berlin-based M-Appeal has boarded “ When I Existed ,” a buzzy, feel-good second-chance drama comedy and Kafkian social satire which proved a standout at the Cannes Market’s Ventana Sur Goes to Cannes showcase, marking an auspicious debut for Uruguay’s Alejandro Damiani and Martin Avdolov.

A select but discerning sales agent of Latin American movies, M-Appeal has picked up international sales on “When I Existed” (“Cuando yo existía”) just weeks before the feature’s world premiere in the Critics’ Picks Competition at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival .

Related Stories

Box Office: 'Other Mommy' Makes $3.6 Million in Previews

Mediawan's Pierre-Antoine Capton on Buying Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine and Doubling Down on Hollywood Amid Consolidation (EXCLUSIVE)

The feature debut of writer-directors by Damiani and Martin Avdolov, “When I Existed” unfolds its humane modern parable when Silvio Bertolini retires after spending 40 years building Uruguay’s foremost gates construction company.

Attempting to draw his pension, and with his credit cards frozen, he discovers that the National Pension and Retirement Fund, also his bank, register him as deceased.

Sent from pillar to post – to the bank’s Accounts, Payments and Claims treading dark puddled basement corridors and joining seemingly interminable lines. He meanwhile reconnects with old friends from his sculling boat club of youth, and re-awakes – but is it too late? – to what it really means to be alive: Spending time with his wife who hopes retirement will open a new chapter in their life together.

Driving “When I Existed” is a notably modulated performance from César Troncoso, star of “The Pope’s Toilet” and “The Eternaut,” as Silvio, ranging from smiling containment of a reasonable man to outraged anger, paralysis from anxiety, wistful regret and lovelorn solitude. Silvia Kutica (“Avellaneda’s Moon,” “Argentina, Land of Love and Revenge”) plays Silvio’s now increasingly estranged wife of 40 years.

“When I Existed” is lead produced by Federico Cetta for Uruguay’s El Cielo Cine who describes as “a story of reinvention built around the things that truly matter.”

Structured as near any film of ambition these days an as international co-production, “When I Existed” is co-produced by David Matamoros at Barcelona’s Doce Entertainment and Andrés Rosenblatt at Montevideo’s Metropolis Films as co-producers. Matías Burgos at Moon Ideas, also based out of Montevideo, serves as associate producer.

“This story speaks to us in a world where we have the constant feeling that time is slipping away between obligations we don’t always choose,” said Avdolov. “What do we do with the time we have? Today we need small acts of resistance against a logic that tends to make everything increasingly automatic and artificial. For me, making this film has something of that.”

“What won us over about ‘When I Existed’ was its rare mix of humor and humanity,” said M-Appeal founder Maren Kroymann.

She added: “Silvio is a charming man who struggles to accept retirement, while his wife has been waiting for this moment, hoping they can finally enjoy life together. Their story is both touching and deeply relatable, reminding us how easily we can get caught up in our habits and lose sight of what matters most. It’s a film that makes you laugh, moves you, and reminds us that it’s never too late to reconnect with the people we love.”

‘When I Existed,’ Broken Down by Damiani and Avdolov

“When I Existed” is shot with unusual elegance but sense of humor by Manuel Branaa, a camera operator on J.A. Bayona’s Netflix smash-hit “Society of the Snow.” This is caught in the the lateral tracking shot with which it opens, crossing a dark granite stone tomb taking in the red and yellows of flowers left on it. Asethetically, it’s a highly pleasing composition, but the flowers are wilting.

Drawing a counterpoint between the open expanses of marshlands, where Silvio catches up with his boat club best friends of youth, the charcoal grey and black corridors and barred doors and windows of the National Pension and Retirement Fund’s labyrinthine office conveys a sense of claustrophobia – that of a man caught not only in a bureaucratic system but his own self-absorption.

“When I Existed” delves into “the nature of the system, the ego, bureaucracy, technological trends, the dangers of alienation, and the erosion of humanity,” said Damiani and Avdolov. “We poured our souls into even the smallest details – things that might go unnoticed by others, but which, to us, made the work feel complete and purposeful,” they added.

Damiani has worked for years in advertising, as a copywriter and designer, wining Uruguay’s fist Golden Lion, then in VFX rising to Creative Director at top Uruguayan VFX house Aparato.

Avdolov has transitioned to filmmaking from a career as a novelist (“Violeta Corazón,” “Camba”), short-story writer and author of the non-fiction “El Corazón Creativo” (“The Creative Heart”).

“When I Existed” is born from the deepest fear any human being can have: how are we supposed to live? No one teaches you that,” Damiani told Variety .

It is also semi-autobiographical. “Working on ‘When I Existed’ made us realize how much of ourselves we poured into the film’s protagonist,” they added. “For many years, we had channeled our energy and creativity into other people’s projects. Following the pandemic – and having passed the age of 40– we decided to commit ourselves to our own meaningful projects. We see this film as a reminder that we are not here to live someone else’s life;

Damiani’s 2016 short, “M.A.M.O.N. (Monitor Against Mexicans Over Nationwide),” went viral, hitting over 13 million views on YouTube.

El Cielo Cine

Of features, “El Cielo Cine” has produced with Argentina 2025’s well-received adopted son drama “Emi,” directed by Ezequiel Erríquez, and Santiago Giralt’s 2023 “Norma,” a later-life self-discovery tale starring and co-written by Mercedes Morán (“Neruda,” “My Sad Dead”) which scored a best comedy Platino Award nomination.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 承载生命的躯体、被时间掏空的脸庞、白雪与墓碑。加里·布里奇尔（Gary Briechle）的新书汇集了长期未曾面世的杰作，堪称今年秋天最令人挥之不去的摄影集。L’article Gary Briechle: “Life makes marks” est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .
