"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加：制作湿版时涉及三个角色：被拍摄者、我和相机。其实，当我提到相机时，我指的是整个过程。大三脚架、大相机、黑布、卡车后面的各种物件。面对这些东西是一种奇特的体验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的工作方式有好几种。一种是经过较多布置的。但对我来说，布置场景并不比街头抓拍逊色。被拍摄者知道有事情正在发生。他们参与其中，而作为摄影师，你依然必须挑选正确的时刻，只不过这与其说是决定性瞬间，不如说是一段决定性的持续时间。照片可能需要持续一秒钟，也可能需要持续三十秒。你必须去感受被拍摄者的状态，同时还要兼顾光线和所有技术细节。但如果你运气好，就能捕捉到某种内在的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在许多肖像中看到了大量空白、缺乏张力的面孔。这让我明白了哪些不该做。眼睛可以非同寻常，我总是格外关注它们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因为这个过程很慢——从头到尾可能需要五分钟左右——人们往往会稍微平静下来。他们从生活中抽离出一分钟，静静坐着。很多人几乎从未真正静止过。他们总是蹦蹦跳跳的。而“静止”是一个有趣的、值得沉浸的领域。对于我认识的一些人来说，保持静止会激发出某种奇妙的东西。也许是某种心理深处的东西。我其实很难解释，但我能看得出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有时候我留在相机后面，这样他们能看到我在那里、参与其中。另一些时候我会稍微走到一旁，请他们看镜头而不是看我。这样一来，照片就更纯粹地关于他们，而较少关乎他们与我之间的关系。他们以某种方式展现了自我。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这台大相机带来了一种严肃感。人们明白这是一项郑重的工序。他们希望配合好，让它顺利完成。所以这些时刻变得很严肃，我喜欢这样。我也曾在生日派对和婚礼上拍过照片，我也很享受那种热闹的乐趣，但我的作品通常带有一种更严肃的质感，而这一工艺与此不无关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的另一种工作方式，特别是在周围有一群人的时候，是对大家说：“嘿，各位，我要装一块底片。如果我走到你旁边，能请你配合保持不动吗？只要一分钟就好。”这在公园或人群聚集的场合特别滑稽。只要有几个人愿意为我作保，这就成了一场小游戏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这让我产生了一种狂热的冲动。在这种情况下觉得能拍出一张照片简直有点荒谬，而我觉得这正是吸引力所在。而且我可以指出几次它确实非常成功的时刻。我的目标总是以这样的作品结束一天：这是我开始这一天时完全无法想象的。这确实把我带到了这里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然后，我在不知道自己要做什么的情况下放上一块底片。我只是走到他们中间，看会发生什么。为什么不呢？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些照片大多拍得并不理想。我可以肯定地说。但当它们成功时，其生动和复杂程度可能是更传统的肖像照所不具备的。这里其实没有什么规则。我正试图把用小型相机工作的一些感觉带入这个笨重的工艺中。带来一些自由，一些即兴。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但这种工艺始终都在场，并参与其中。它是拍摄这张照片的第三个角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-01-1024x664.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle，选自《I Want To See A Lighthouse》，由 Charcoal Press 出版", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你在转向摄影之前曾当过多年雕塑家。当你从物质转向光线时，你看世界的方式发生了什么转变？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加里·布里希尔：是的，从十五岁左右开始，雕塑是我的重心，持续了大约二十年。我喜欢木头、石头和铸件，而且我相当关注物体的表面。后来，我对事物的形态变得更加感兴趣。我在摄影中依然能看到这种区别。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一张分辨率极高的数码影像可以向你展示脸部的绝大部分表面。但形态——如果你要去雕刻那张脸或者用粘土制作它——则关乎头部和脸部本身的体积。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我喜欢湿版胶棉摄影的原因在于，你可以在同一块底片上兼得这两者。你能获得这种强烈的细节刻画，而当某人在长时间曝光期间稍微移动、在空间中稍微转动时，你就能看到形态、属于它的雕塑感。在我的眼中，胶棉工艺天然倾向于形态，部分原因正是由于长时间曝光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于雕塑，你制作的是单一的物件。你可能会达到一个你认为完成了而且你很喜欢的阶段。或者你可能并不是特别喜欢它，但你也不会把它扔掉。无论如何，总会有这样一个时刻，你选择继续往前走。然后它就在那里：你制作的一个物件。一件雕塑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我把这种态度带到了一部分的印相中。我喜欢玻璃底片印相的效果，但我通常只想制作一幅或两幅印相。我知道我可以做成一个版数。然而对我而言，制作一个版数感觉有点浪费时间。我喜欢独一无二的一张，最多两张。我通常会把印相送给给我当模特或与我合作的人，这基本上就是我的做法。我对摄影中的孤品完全能够接受。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我意识到这有点抽象，但在雕塑和摄影中，形态与表面的刻画对我而言始终在起作用。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当然，雕塑是用双手制作的，至少我喜欢的那种是这样。胶棉工艺同样非常注重双手操作。我不禁想到，我用双手和身体参与得越多，这件作品对我而言就越有意义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有时，一张数码照片会让人觉得它是被我拿在面前的这个小盒子制作出来的，而不是由我制作的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-29-1024x760.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle，选自《I Want To See A Lighthouse》，由 Charcoal Press 出版", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《I Want To See A Lighthouse》中，许多影像以最毫不留情面的真实展现了身体：见证了时间的皮肤，被生活磨损的肉体。究竟是什么吸引你走向这些疲惫的身体和饱经风霜的脸庞？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加里·布里希尔：我们来比较两把锤子。一把来自家居建材店（Home Depot）。另一把来自埃尔默谷仓（Elmer’s Barn），那是一个旧货店，里面有很多价格便宜的东西。没什么太花哨的东西。我觉得这是一个非常能带来灵感的场所。你拿起的几乎每件东西都显示出某些人类双手的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "至于家居建材店，嗯，我们都知道家居建材店。那把锤子有一个蓝色的手柄，钢制的锤头和锤柄是一体成型的。锤头并没有连接到任何东西上。里面有工程设计。你能感觉到有人琢磨过如何把手腕的挥甩转化为击打的力量。这把锤子我放在我的作坊里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而那把来自埃尔默谷仓、我放在车里的锤子，则有着金属锤头和直木柄。锤头有着极美的包浆，那是只有时间才能在金属上雕刻出来的痕迹。这不是生锈。里面有蓝色、灰色和木炭色，它们似乎是从金属内部透出来的，而不是浮在表面上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而木质手柄简直复杂得令人难以置信。有木纹，有来自双手或它曾待过的作坊的油污。有一些油漆飞溅的痕迹。有些切口看起来像是手柄曾挡住了它本不该靠近的锯子的去路。还有我辨认不清的某人的首字母缩写。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在某个时刻，锤头变松了，于是有人在手柄末端楔入了一个木楔来把它拧紧。后来那个一定又松了，因为有人在木楔旁边钉入了一枚钉子。这是为了让锤头发紧而做的又一次尝试。你可以看到这一切。有人一直在使用这个东西，并不断寻找让它继续发挥作用的方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为一个人无法刻意制造出那么美丽的锤子。字面意义上说。你可以制造出一把漂亮的锤子，但你无法将所有那些时间倾注其中。所有那些发生在它身上的琐碎细节，它的复杂性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "世上仅存一把来自埃尔默谷仓的这种锤子。而家居建材店的那些则有成千上万把。摄影永远关乎具体性。你努力去寻找某种独特而具有启示意义的东西。这就是工作所在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-21-1024x750.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle，选自《I Want To See A Lighthouse》，由 Charcoal Press 出版", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而这也是湿版工艺对一个人所能做到的。它能将皮肤——一张脸、一条手臂、一只手——呈现为因时间而充满生机的存在。你能在其中看到生命。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这在孩子的皮肤上同样适用。时间以另一种方式存在于那里。那种光滑度，那种几乎如同瓷器般的质感。当然，它不是那把历经沧桑的老锤子。但这里有形态与深度，光线会找到它们。它向你展示了关于在那种皮肤中活着的某些东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "生活留下了印记。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "书里有一张照片，拍的是一个婴儿坐在放在墓地中央的汽车安全座椅上，在那里，出生与死亡被定格在同一个画框里。你在这种碰撞中寻找什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加·布里希尔（G.B.）：我和一个朋友带着她的宝宝在墓地里。有些墓碑非常宏伟。有几块上面雕刻着骷髅和交叉骨，在那种地方遇到这个还挺奇特的。很有蒂姆·伯顿（Tim Burton）的风格。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我带了一些硅胶模具材料来制作翻模。（而且我觉得我应该说明一下——硅胶完整地揭下来了。没有残留，没有痕迹，对那里的一切保持着尊重。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这张照片就这样自然而然地出现了，就像它们有时会发生的那样。一点也不隐晦。墓地里的婴儿。两头的事物，就在那里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我喜欢这块湿版呈现出的婴儿和汽车安全座椅的洁白质感，景深也感觉恰到好处。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我总是不由自主地在婴儿身上看到我们所有人。那种脆弱感是如此清晰。到了成年人身上，它就被种种事物埋藏起来了。我们会流露出其中的一部分，或者我们会找到谈论它的方式，但通常都非常吝啬。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但我认为它依然在那里。我们只是有了更多的时间把它掩盖起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的肖像照带有一种深沉的亲密感，仿佛你的拍摄对象在某种意义上就是家人。你和被拍摄者之间这种情感上或身体上的亲密感是如何产生的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加·布里希尔（G.B.）：相机是镜头前的人与镜头后的人之间的等号。来回传递的能量是脆弱与爱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在用湿版拍摄缅因州之后，你曾用彩色胶片拍摄过缅因州，然后在这第三本书中又回到了黑白。是什么让你重新回到了黑白？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加·布里希尔（G.B.）：摄影的历史相当短，从1840年前后开始，当然还有此前的一切。我对这一切都很感兴趣。我想尝试一切，我也差不多都试过了。不过，达盖尔摄影法（daguerreotypes）里涉及的汞差不多把那条路给堵死了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "针孔相机让我着迷。一个暗盒基本上就能满足你百分之九十的需求。由于雕塑出身，制作相机成了我进入摄影的途径。我立刻就开始制作针孔相机，我想这从一开始就赋予了我一种“一次只拍一张”的态度。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这从来都不是关于一天能拍多少。而是关于保持专注、挑出某个事物，并且接受只拍一张或两张照片。如果能多拍点也行。如果没有拍到什么，只要好好观察了一番，那也依然可以是美好的一天。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一方面，湿版看起来非常复杂；但另一方面，它也有着某种相当简单的地方。有一个镜头、一个暗盒、光线，以及对光线作出反应的银。我依然能感受到与那些早期针孔相机的联系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-23-1024x738.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle，选自《I Want To See A Lighthouse》，由 Charcoal Press 出版", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "话虽如此，在我做湿版的很大一部分时间里，我的脖子上也挂着一台徕卡（Leica）。我会在屋子旁边忙着弄湿版，孩子们在蹦床上玩耍，然后我会想：我在那边干什么呢？照片都在那边。有时我甚至会把湿版留在相机里晾干，然后拿着徕卡走过去。我当然在里面用 Tri-X 胶卷。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但在经历了几年的黑白摄影后，我对彩色产生了兴趣。富士普维亚（Fuji Provia）是我特别喜欢的一种。它有着这种质朴、安静的色彩。维尔维亚（Velvia）有时会给人一种对我大喊大叫的感觉。普维亚则不会。而且它是幻灯片胶卷，所以你去商店把这些小照片拿回来时，它们都安在片夹里。像一颗颗绚丽的小宝石。我真的很喜欢那样。用它的时候我自己冲洗 C-41，但我从来没涉足过幻灯片的冲洗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当这本黑白书即将收尾、杰克·伍迪（Jack Woody）基本上拿到了他需要的所有东西并正在编排顺序时，我给他寄了两百张普维亚彩色照片冲印件。我说：“这些不是为了这本书，但也许它们能让你对我拍摄的人有更多了解，或者能传达出单靠黑白所无法表现的东西。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他回邮件说：“嗯，我觉得这应该是你的第二本书。”那真是一个巨大的惊喜。我完全没有料到。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但事情一直在变。最终，要找到幻灯片冲洗服务变得越来越难，我便渐渐疏远了它。我转向了数码，而且我至今仍随身携带数码相机。有时我想要尽可能多的细节描述。比如那种连睫毛都能数得清的肖像。在某些时候，我觉得那种感觉很对。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但我基本上还是回到了湿版摄影，偶尔夹杂一点彩色。管理数码作品快把我逼疯了。曾有一台相机连同存有我从未导出的照片的存储卡一起从车里被偷走了。那些就这么没了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而且即使对于我保留下来的照片，我也从来找不到任何东西。我会备份、把它们存在不同的硬盘上，结果东西多到我最后根本不知道自己到底有什么了。实际上，我干什么事都差不多是这样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这不再有趣了。而且我觉得去追寻有趣的东西、或者追寻感觉最好的东西，没什么好羞耻的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不想把所有时间都花在为了整理东西而自我折磨上。这些时间本可以用来创作或观察。相反，我却在摆弄一个需要更新的程序、或者某个与其他软件停止兼容的东西、或者是那种需要价值600美元墨水并对我说“对不起，在您安装新的维护墨盒之前我无法为您工作”的打印机。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这让我筋疲力尽。这对我来说感觉一点也不人性化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于湿版，我依然喜欢身临其境、亲自动手的感觉。对我来说，那种体验简直无可匹敌。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "我真的很喜欢我拍摄的人。我认识很多人，甚至已经超过20年了，我知道他们会在书中看到自己时感到兴奋。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对我来说，一个巨大的障碍是试图谈论我的作品。从某种意义上说，其实没多少可谈的。我认为事物可以纯粹以视觉形式存在，那就足够了。而且我不怎么擅长交际。我喜欢在场外，比起上场比赛，我更喜欢在一旁看比赛。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我拍摄的每一个人，我都会为画中人冲印一张照片。那些就像微型展览。本人能看到自己，他们的女朋友能看到他们，他们的父母和一些朋友也能看到他们。所以在某种程度上，在过去的30年里，我办了成百上千个微型展览，能够把照片送给别人，这种感觉太棒了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我觉得偶尔办一次展览感觉挺好。你可以对父母说：“看，我可没完全疯。”但我觉得为了工作而进行交际、套近乎、大谈艺术空话，感觉不如脚踏实地做创作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对我而言，书就是终极的展览。因此，杰西能来做这本书，我感到非常高兴和幸运。而且这是一本很大的书。如果可以的话，我希望每8到10年左右出一本书，这就足够了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这挺有意思的。装玻璃底片的盒子非常重。一个小盒子里通常竖直放着80或90张5×7英寸的底片，通常是木制的。把它们全放在一组书架上或同一个地方，感觉总是不太对。它们实在太重了，所以我把它们放在房子的各个角落。算是把重量分散开来吧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "把东西拿出来给杰西看，简直快把我折腾疯了，因为我对自己的作品像个陌生人一样，根本不知道它们在哪。我不知道盒子里到底有什么。这让人沮丧，但同时也挺好玩的。就好像，哦对，我记得那张。杰西说他很喜欢我们俩一起第一次看到这些影像的感觉。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想我只是在做我想做的事。这是一种偏好。在交际、交谈、搞画廊活动和真正埋头创作之间，其实没多少好纠结的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想我只是喜欢真正去做创作。我真的真的很喜欢做创作。这是一种生活方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这本书里没有出现任何灯塔，然而书名却依然是：《我想看一座灯塔》（I Want To See A Lighthouse），它源自一个孩子的心愿。为什么这些影像会配上这样一个书名？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加·布里希尔：在摄影中，你与世界存在着某种联系。你并不是孤立的。你在对周围的事物做出回应。它始于辨识：这里有什么东西值得一看，值得花时间去思考。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "多年前，我在罗克兰旧物仓储店的地上发现了一个孩子的笔记本。那是人们把觉得自己用不上、别人可能想要的东西留在那里的地方，而其他人则会来这里看看有什么能用的。我不知道这本笔记本是谁的。其中一页上写着：“我想看一座灯塔。”这似乎是猜字游戏的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "缅因州有着岩石密布的海岸，常常隐匿在迷雾之中。到处都有灯塔。我们已经习惯把它们当作装饰品——日历和咖啡杯上的图片。人们很容易忘记它们原本存在的意义。身处水上、面临危险的人需要看到一束光。他们需要一条通往安全港湾的路。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想我们现在都需要这个。有时感觉整个世界都需要。情况真的非常危急。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但笔记本上的那句话是猜字游戏的一部分。在左上角，你可以看到那个画了一半的小人。这改变了我对这些文字的理解。我们依然有机会找到灯塔，但剩下的猜测机会已经不多了。你必须在还来得及的时候找到它。而这是一个孩子写的。一个孩子想要找到一座灯塔。这说明了我们施加给孩子的焦虑究竟是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当你翻过那一页，还有另一张带横线的纸，上面用深色铅笔涂抹着阴影。黑色正在向白色合围。我不知道这个孩子的意图是什么，也不知道这两页之间是否有任何关联。但我忍不住把它们联系在一起看。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我看来，它们传达着相同的情感：光芒依然存在，而留给我们去寻找它的时间只有那么多。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-06-1024x801.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© 加·布里希尔（Gary Briechle），选自《我想看一座灯塔》（I Want To See A Lighthouse），由 Charcoal Press 出版", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的作品有时会被拿来与拉ルフ·尤金·米蒂亚德（Ralph Eugene Meatyard）的作品作比较，因为其中流露出一种奇异感；或者与黛安·阿勃丝（Diane Arbus）相比，因为她那正面的凝视以及反复出现的双胞胎。我还要加上罗杰·拜伦（Roger Ballen），因为那些稚拙的涂鸦、骨头以及深邃的黑白世界。有没有哪位艺术家，无论是摄影师、画家还是作家，他们的作品在特定层面上启发了你？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加·布里希尔：黛安·阿勃丝对我的影响最大。我对她的个人专集、书籍《启示》（Revelations）以及《无题》（Untitled）非常熟悉。我很喜欢她在《Revelations》一书中的文字。你可以从她列清单的方式中看出那种狂热。我对此深有共鸣。在我看来，她在专集中的引语是有史以来关于摄影最好的文字之一。她完美诠释了什么是“全力以赴”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我第一次看到她的作品时，并不理解她是如何拍出这些照片的。但随着时间推移，我脑海中形成了一个画面：她独自坐在一列开往某处的火车上。旁边有一列与她平行的火车，上面坐满了人。不知为何，两列火车在站台上非常短暂地停了一下，两边的车门同时打开，她看到了车里的人。真的只有眨眼之间。接着车门关上，火车继续前行。我有一种使了个眼色或眨了下眼的感觉，但她拿着相机站在那里，得以进入这个平行的世界。我记得当时想，“我想看看那个世界，”却完全不知道该怎么做到。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着时间推移，我偶尔能窥见一鳞半爪。这仍然是个谜，但我知道它确实会发生。我拍的大多数东西都是垃圾，简直是丢脸到极点的垃圾，就算它占到98%吧。但我确实抓住了车门打开的瞬间。这就足够了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿勃丝身上有一种纯粹性。我非常崇拜她。我知道“真实”这个词在摄影中饱受诟病。这就跟个笑话一样，摄影不真实是显而易见的。我想，比如说你在耶鲁的考试上说“黛安·阿勃丝说的是实话”，你的分数可能会受点影响，但在我看来，她的作品中无疑蕴含着一种超越批评的个人与心理真实。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "迪斯法默表面上看起来如此平淡，却有着无与伦比的敏感。我极度喜欢埃格尔斯顿，他很古怪。观察入微的影像。他就是全身心投入的代名词。马克·科恩在街头创作的方式太感人了。感觉火车上的车门为他频繁地敞开着。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加里·布里奇尔（Gary Briechle）著的《我想去看灯塔》（I Want To See A Lighthouse）由 Charcoal Press 于 2026 年出版。精装，亚麻封面，配有嵌入式图像，224 页，11 × 14 英寸，售价 85 美元。", "links": [{"text": "I Want To See A Lighthouse", "url": "https://charcoalpress.com/shop/i-want-to-see-a-lighthouse"}, {"text": "Charcoal Press", "url": "https://charcoalpress.com"}], "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gary Briechle’s Maine is nothing like a postcard. Long settled in Rockland, a small working port on the East Coast, the American photographer works in wet plate collodion, a rare and demanding process. For thirty years he has photographed his family, his friends, his neighbors. From each plate he makes a single print, which he gives to his sitter, before the glass is put away in the recesses of his house. His third book, I Want To See A Lighthouse , published by Charcoal Press, finally brings this work out of the dark. Interview."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Your photographs dwell in harsh territory: precariousness, aging, death hovering at the edge of things. Where does this attentiveness to the fragility of existence come from?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gary Briechle: Our time here is finite. Being here has to mean something. Pressure’s on."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That’s why I stay busy. I shoot. If I see something I want to photograph, I do it right then. I don’t tell myself I’ll come back to it later, because later is a question mark. Every day counts. It’s kind of a pain in the ass, it’s always been hard to relax for me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I think of life as a line, mostly moving from left to right. It isn’t perfectly straight. And there are loops, stutters, slow and fast. But the direction is clear. Birth is one bookend. Death is the other. In between are the books, the chapters, and the pages—the things we do while we’re here. And on some of those pages are pictures."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I can feel the pressure. I hate myself when I waste a day. But that feeling becomes a powerful motivator for the next day. If I can help it, I never want to let two of those wasted days happen in a row."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My father died at ninety-nine. His mind was still pretty much there. I would look at him and wonder what he had been like as a child. Not in some abstract way—I wanted to see that child inside the old man sitting in front of me. There were photographs in boxes that had been passed down, so I had somewhere to begin. I could look at his face at ninety-nine, then look at a picture of him at five, and feel the connection."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The child and the old man are not opposites. They’re the same life, carried forward. They’re both fragile. They’re both vulnerable. They both need other people. I need help myself, honestly."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Maybe life isn’t a line at all. Maybe it’s a cluster of experiences, events, influences, actions, reactions, things we do, and things done to us. We gather all of it, no sorting. Why bother? We carry it around somehow."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So I shoot. I put things in the box while I can."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There is no denying the relationship between time and photography. The constant flow stops on a dime here and there, and we can look, contemplate, and feel in some saturated rich way, the way movies make us feel or music. Then we start moving again."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-19-711x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-20-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wet plate collodion demands a kind of ceremony: coating the glass, asking your subject to hold still for long seconds. What passes between you and the person you are photographing in that suspended time?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "G.B.: There are three characters involved in making a wet plate: the subject, me, and the camera. And really, when I say the camera, I mean the whole process. The big tripod, the big camera, the dark cloth, stuff in the back of the truck. It’s a strange thing to be in front of."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I work in a couple of ways. One is more a set up. But for me, setting something up isn’t any less authentic than street shooting. The subject knows something is happening. They’re participating, and as the photographer, you still have to pick the right moment, except it’s less a decisive moment and more a decisive duration. The picture might need to last a second, or it might need to last thirty seconds. You have to feel where the subject is, along with figuring out the light and all the technical things. But if you’re lucky you get something inward."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I see a lot of blankness, muscleless faces in many portraits. It shows me what not to do. Eyes can be extraordinary and I always pay attention to them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Because the process is slow—start to finish might take five minutes or so—people tend to settle down a little. They pull out of life for a minute and sit still. A lot of people are hardly ever still. They’re always bouncing around. And stillness is an interesting thing to dip into. With some people I know, being still brings out something marvelous. Something psychologically deep, maybe. I don’t really know how to explain it, but I can see it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sometimes I stay behind the camera so they see me there, involved. Other times I move a little to the side and ask them to look at the camera instead of at me. Then it becomes more a picture about them, and less about their relationship with me. They present themselves somehow."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And the big camera brings a seriousness to it. People understand this is involved. They want to help it work out. So these become serious moments, and I like that. I’ve made pictures at birthday parties, and weddings, and I love the fun of that too, but my work generally has a more serious feeling, and the process has something to do with that."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The other way I work, especially when there’s a group of people around, is to say, “Hey, guys, I’m going to put a plate in. If I come up to you, can I ask you to hold still? It’ll only take a minute.” This is particularly funny in a park or some gathering of people. And as long as there’s a few people that will vouch for me, it’s a bit of a game."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I get a manic spike out of this. It’s kind of absurd to think a picture will come out under these circumstances, and I think that’s the attraction. And also I can point to times it worked really well. The goal is always to wind up the day with something I couldn’t have imagined when I started the day. This has gotten me there for sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Then I put a plate in without knowing what I’m going to do. I just go out among them and see what happens. Why not?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mostly those pictures don’t work. I’d say that for sure. But when they do, they can be very alive and complex in a way that a more conventional portrait might not be. There aren’t really any rules to this. I’m trying to bring some of the feeling of working with a small camera into this cumbersome process. Some freedom, some spontaneity."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But the process is always there, participating. It’s the third character making the photograph."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-01-1024x664.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You spent years as a sculptor before turning to photography. What shifted in the way you saw the world when you moved from matter to light?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "G.B.: Yes, sculpture was my focus starting around the age of fifteen, for about twenty years. I liked wood and stone and castings, and I was pretty involved with the surface of objects. Later, I became more interested in the form of things. I still see that distinction in photography."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A really high-resolution digital image can show you so much of the surface of a face. But the form—if you were going to carve that face or make it out of clay—is about the volume of the head, the face itself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What I love about wet plate is that you can get both on the same plate. You get this intense description, but when someone moves a little during a long exposure, turns a little in space, you can see the form, the sculpture of it. To my eye, collodion has that tendency toward form, partly because of the long exposures."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With sculpture, you make one thing. You might get to a point where you’re done and you like it. Or you might not really like it, but you don’t throw it out. Either way, there’s a point where you move on. And there it is: one thing you made. One sculpture."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I carry some of that into printmaking. I love how glass negatives print, but I usually only want to make one or two prints. I know I could make an edition. For me, though, making an edition feels like a bit of a waste of time. I like the uniqueness of one, maybe two. I usually give a print to the person who sat for me or worked with me, so that’s generally what I do. I’m completely fine with a one-off in photography."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I realize this is a little abstract, but form and surface description are always in play for me, in both sculpture and photography."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And of course sculpture is made with your hands, at least the kind I like. Collodion is very hands-on too. I can’t help thinking that the more involved I am with my hands and my body, the more meaningful the work is to me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sometimes a digital picture can feel like it was made by this box I’m holding in front of me, rather than by me."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-29-1024x760.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In I Want To See A Lighthouse , many of the images show bodies in their most unsparing truth: skin that bears witness to time, flesh worn down by living. What draws you, precisely, to these tired bodies and bruised faces?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "G.B.: Let’s compare two hammers. One comes from Home Depot. The other comes from Elmer’s Barn, which is an antiques group shop with a lot of inexpensive things. Not much fancy stuff. I find it a very inspiring place. Almost everything you pick up shows some evidence of somebody’s hands."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Home Depot, well, we all know Home Depot. The hammer has a blue handle, and the steel head and shaft are one piece. The head doesn’t attach to anything. There’s engineering in it. You can feel that somebody figured out how to take that whip of your hand and turn it into the power of the hit. This hammer I have in my shop."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Now, the hammer from Elmer’s I keep in the car has a metal head and a straight wooden handle. The head has this gorgeous patina, the kind of thing only time can make on metal. It’s not rust. There are blues and grays and charcoal colors, and they seem to come from inside the metal rather than sit on the surface."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And the wooden handle is just unbelievably complex. There’s the grain, and there’s oil from hands, or from the shop it lived in. There’s some paint splatter. There are cuts where it looks like the handle got in the path of a saw it shouldn’t have been near. Someone’s initials I can’t make out."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At some point the head got loose, so somebody drove a wedge into the end of the handle to tighten it. Then that must have loosened up, because somebody drove a nail in beside the wedge. Another attempt to keep the head on tight. You can see all of that. Somebody kept using this thing and kept finding ways to make it work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I don’t think a person can deliberately make a hammer that beautiful. Literally. You could make a beautiful hammer, but you couldn’t put all that time into it. All those little things that happened to it, the complexity of it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There’s only one of those hammers from Elmer’s Barn in existence. There’s tens of thousands of them from Home Depot. Photography is always about being specific. You try to find something unique and revelatory. That’s the job."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lighthouse-21-1024x750.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And that’s something that wet plate can do with a person. It can show skin—a face, an arm, a hand—as something alive with time. You can see life there."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That’s true of a child’s skin too. Time is there in a different way. There’s that smoothness, that almost porcelain quality. Of course, it isn’t the old, weathered hammer. But there’s form and depth, and the light finds it. It shows you something about being alive in that skin."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Life makes marks."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There is a photograph in this book of an infant in a car seat set down in the middle of a cemetery, where birth and death are held in the same frame. What do you seek in this kind of collision?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "G.B.: I was with a friend and her baby in a graveyard. Some of the headstones were magnificent. A few had skulls and crossbones carved into them, which is a pretty bizarre thing to come across. article_text:
Gary Briechle’s Maine is nothing like a postcard. Long settled in Rockland, a small working port on the East Coast, the American photographer works in wet plate collodion, a rare and demanding process. For thirty years he has photographed his family, his friends, his neighbors. From each plate he makes a single print, which he gives to his sitter, before the glass is put away in the recesses of his house. His third book, I Want To See A Lighthouse , published by Charcoal Press, finally brings this work out of the dark. Interview.

Your photographs dwell in harsh territory: precariousness, aging, death hovering at the edge of things. Where does this attentiveness to the fragility of existence come from?

Gary Briechle: Our time here is finite. Being here has to mean something. Pressure’s on.

That’s why I stay busy. I shoot. If I see something I want to photograph, I do it right then. I don’t tell myself I’ll come back to it later, because later is a question mark. Every day counts. It’s kind of a pain in the ass, it’s always been hard to relax for me.

I think of life as a line, mostly moving from left to right. It isn’t perfectly straight. And there are loops, stutters, slow and fast. But the direction is clear. Birth is one bookend. Death is the other. In between are the books, the chapters, and the pages—the things we do while we’re here. And on some of those pages are pictures.

I can feel the pressure. I hate myself when I waste a day. But that feeling becomes a powerful motivator for the next day. If I can help it, I never want to let two of those wasted days happen in a row.

My father died at ninety-nine. His mind was still pretty much there. I would look at him and wonder what he had been like as a child. Not in some abstract way—I wanted to see that child inside the old man sitting in front of me. There were photographs in boxes that had been passed down, so I had somewhere to begin. I could look at his face at ninety-nine, then look at a picture of him at five, and feel the connection.

The child and the old man are not opposites. They’re the same life, carried forward. They’re both fragile. They’re both vulnerable. They both need other people. I need help myself, honestly.

Maybe life isn’t a line at all. Maybe it’s a cluster of experiences, events, influences, actions, reactions, things we do, and things done to us. We gather all of it, no sorting. Why bother? We carry it around somehow.

So I shoot. I put things in the box while I can.

There is no denying the relationship between time and photography. The constant flow stops on a dime here and there, and we can look, contemplate, and feel in some saturated rich way, the way movies make us feel or music. Then we start moving again.

Wet plate collodion demands a kind of ceremony: coating the glass, asking your subject to hold still for long seconds. What passes between you and the person you are photographing in that suspended time?

G.B.: There are three characters involved in making a wet plate: the subject, me, and the camera. And really, when I say the camera, I mean the whole process. The big tripod, the big camera, the dark cloth, stuff in the back of the truck. It’s a strange thing to be in front of.

I work in a couple of ways. One is more a set up. But for me, setting something up isn’t any less authentic than street shooting. The subject knows something is happening. They’re participating, and as the photographer, you still have to pick the right moment, except it’s less a decisive moment and more a decisive duration. The picture might need to last a second, or it might need to last thirty seconds. You have to feel where the subject is, along with figuring out the light and all the technical things. But if you’re lucky you get something inward.

I see a lot of blankness, muscleless faces in many portraits. It shows me what not to do. Eyes can be extraordinary and I always pay attention to them.

Because the process is slow—start to finish might take five minutes or so—people tend to settle down a little. They pull out of life for a minute and sit still. A lot of people are hardly ever still. They’re always bouncing around. And stillness is an interesting thing to dip into. With some people I know, being still brings out something marvelous. Something psychologically deep, maybe. I don’t really know how to explain it, but I can see it.

Sometimes I stay behind the camera so they see me there, involved. Other times I move a little to the side and ask them to look at the camera instead of at me. Then it becomes more a picture about them, and less about their relationship with me. They present themselves somehow.

And the big camera brings a seriousness to it. People understand this is involved. They want to help it work out. So these become serious moments, and I like that. I’ve made pictures at birthday parties, and weddings, and I love the fun of that too, but my work generally has a more serious feeling, and the process has something to do with that.

The other way I work, especially when there’s a group of people around, is to say, “Hey, guys, I’m going to put a plate in. If I come up to you, can I ask you to hold still? It’ll only take a minute.” This is particularly funny in a park or some gathering of people. And as long as there’s a few people that will vouch for me, it’s a bit of a game.

I get a manic spike out of this. It’s kind of absurd to think a picture will come out under these circumstances, and I think that’s the attraction. And also I can point to times it worked really well. The goal is always to wind up the day with something I couldn’t have imagined when I started the day. This has gotten me there for sure.

Then I put a plate in without knowing what I’m going to do. I just go out among them and see what happens. Why not?

Mostly those pictures don’t work. I’d say that for sure. But when they do, they can be very alive and complex in a way that a more conventional portrait might not be. There aren’t really any rules to this. I’m trying to bring some of the feeling of working with a small camera into this cumbersome process. Some freedom, some spontaneity.

But the process is always there, participating. It’s the third character making the photograph.

You spent years as a sculptor before turning to photography. What shifted in the way you saw the world when you moved from matter to light?

G.B.: Yes, sculpture was my focus starting around the age of fifteen, for about twenty years. I liked wood and stone and castings, and I was pretty involved with the surface of objects. Later, I became more interested in the form of things. I still see that distinction in photography.

A really high-resolution digital image can show you so much of the surface of a face. But the form—if you were going to carve that face or make it out of clay—is about the volume of the head, the face itself.

What I love about wet plate is that you can get both on the same plate. You get this intense description, but when someone moves a little during a long exposure, turns a little in space, you can see the form, the sculpture of it. To my eye, collodion has that tendency toward form, partly because of the long exposures.

With sculpture, you make one thing. You might get to a point where you’re done and you like it. Or you might not really like it, but you don’t throw it out. Either way, there’s a point where you move on. And there it is: one thing you made. One sculpture.

I carry some of that into printmaking. I love how glass negatives print, but I usually only want to make one or two prints. I know I could make an edition. For me, though, making an edition feels like a bit of a waste of time. I like the uniqueness of one, maybe two. I usually give a print to the person who sat for me or worked with me, so that’s generally what I do. I’m completely fine with a one-off in photography.

I realize this is a little abstract, but form and surface description are always in play for me, in both sculpture and photography.

And of course sculpture is made with your hands, at least the kind I like. Collodion is very hands-on too. I can’t help thinking that the more involved I am with my hands and my body, the more meaningful the work is to me.

Sometimes a digital picture can feel like it was made by this box I’m holding in front of me, rather than by me.

In I Want To See A Lighthouse , many of the images show bodies in their most unsparing truth: skin that bears witness to time, flesh worn down by living. What draws you, precisely, to these tired bodies and bruised faces?

G.B.: Let’s compare two hammers. One comes from Home Depot. The other comes from Elmer’s Barn, which is an antiques group shop with a lot of inexpensive things. Not much fancy stuff. I find it a very inspiring place. Almost everything you pick up shows some evidence of somebody’s hands.

Home Depot, well, we all know Home Depot. The hammer has a blue handle, and the steel head and shaft are one piece. The head doesn’t attach to anything. There’s engineering in it. You can feel that somebody figured out how to take that whip of your hand and turn it into the power of the hit. This hammer I have in my shop.

Now, the hammer from Elmer’s I keep in the car has a metal head and a straight wooden handle. The head has this gorgeous patina, the kind of thing only time can make on metal. It’s not rust. There are blues and grays and charcoal colors, and they seem to come from inside the metal rather than sit on the surface.

And the wooden handle is just unbelievably complex. There’s the grain, and there’s oil from hands, or from the shop it lived in. There’s some paint splatter. There are cuts where it looks like the handle got in the path of a saw it shouldn’t have been near. Someone’s initials I can’t make out.

At some point the head got loose, so somebody drove a wedge into the end of the handle to tighten it. Then that must have loosened up, because somebody drove a nail in beside the wedge. Another attempt to keep the head on tight. You can see all of that. Somebody kept using this thing and kept finding ways to make it work.

I don’t think a person can deliberately make a hammer that beautiful. Literally. You could make a beautiful hammer, but you couldn’t put all that time into it. All those little things that happened to it, the complexity of it.

There’s only one of those hammers from Elmer’s Barn in existence. There’s tens of thousands of them from Home Depot. Photography is always about being specific. You try to find something unique and revelatory. That’s the job.

And that’s something that wet plate can do with a person. It can show skin—a face, an arm, a hand—as something alive with time. You can see life there.

That’s true of a child’s skin too. Time is there in a different way. There’s that smoothness, that almost porcelain quality. Of course, it isn’t the old, weathered hammer. But there’s form and depth, and the light finds it. It shows you something about being alive in that skin.

Life makes marks.

There is a photograph in this book of an infant in a car seat set down in the middle of a cemetery, where birth and death are held in the same frame. What do you seek in this kind of collision?

G.B.: I was with a friend and her baby in a graveyard. Some of the headstones were magnificent. A few had skulls and crossbones carved into them, which is a pretty bizarre thing to come across. Pretty Tim Burton.

I had some silicone molding material to make castings. (And I feel like I should say—the silicone lifted off completely. No residue, no marks, respectful of what was there.)

And the picture just presented itself, like they sometimes do. Nothing very subtle about it. A baby in a graveyard. There were the bookends, right there.

I liked how the plate rendered the whiteness of the baby and the car seat, and depth of field felt right.

I can’t help seeing all of us in a baby. The vulnerability is so clear. With adults, it gets buried under things. We let some of it show, or we find a way to talk about it, but usually pretty sparingly.

But I think it’s still there. We’ve just had more time to cover it up.

There is a quality of deep intimacy in your portraits, as though your subjects were, in some sense, family. What accounts for that closeness, emotional or physical, between you and the people you photograph?

G.B.: The camera is the equal sign between who is in front of it and who is behind it. The energy that passes back and forth is vulnerability and love.

After Gary Briechle in collodion, you made Maine in color, before returning to black and white for this third book. What brought you back to it?

G.B.: Photography has a pretty short history, starting around 1840, give or take, and of course there’s everything that led up to it. I was interested in all of it. I wanted to try everything, and I pretty much did. The mercury involved in daguerreotypes kind of put the kibosh on that one, though.

Pinhole cameras fascinated me. A dark container is about ninety percent of what you need. Coming from sculpture, building cameras was a way into photography. I started making pinhole cameras right away, and I think that gave me a one-at-a-time attitude from the beginning.

It was never really about how much I could shoot in a day. It was about paying attention, picking something out, and being okay with making one or two pictures. More if it happened. And if I didn’t make any, it could still be a good day if I’d done some good looking.

Wet plate seems very complicated on the one hand, but there’s something pretty simple about it, too. There’s a lens, a box, light, and silver that responds to the light. I can still feel the connection to those first pinhole cameras.

That said, a lot of the time I was doing wet plate, I also had a Leica around my neck. I’d be busy with a plate over by the side of the house, and the kids would be playing on the trampoline, and I’d think, What am I doing over here? The pictures are over there. Sometimes I’d just leave the plate sitting in the camera to dry out and walk over with the Leica. I shot Tri-X in it, of course.

But after years of black-and-white, I got interested in color. Fuji Provia was a particular favorite. It had this plain, quiet color. Velvia could feel like it was shouting at me. Provia didn’t. And it was slide film, so you’d go to the store and get these little pictures back in their mounts. Little spectacular gems. I really liked that. I developed my own C-41 when I used it, but I never got into processing slides.

When the black-and-white book was wrapping up and Jack Woody had pretty much everything he needed, and was developing the sequence, I sent him a couple hundred prints from the Provia pictures. I said, “These aren’t for the book, but maybe they’ll tell you a little more about the people I photograph, or something that doesn’t come across in the black-and-white alone.”

He emailed back and said, “Well, I think this should be your second book.” That was a wow, for sure. I hadn’t expected that.

But things keep changing. Eventually it got harder to find slide processing, and I drifted away from it. I went into digital, and I still carry a digital camera. Sometimes I want all the description I can get. A portrait where you can count the eyelashes. There are times when that feels right to me.

But I’ve mostly come back to collodion, with a little color here and there. Keeping track of the digital work drove me crazy. I had a camera stolen out of the car with a card full of pictures I’d never taken off. Those were just gone.

And even with the pictures I still had, I could never find anything. I’d back things up, put them on different drives, and eventually there was so much stuff that I didn’t really know what I had anymore. Actually, that’s kind of the case with everything with me.

It stopped being fun. And I don’t think there’s any shame in going where the fun is. Or the thing that feels the best.

I don’t want to spend all my time beating myself up about keeping track of things. It’s time I could be making something, or looking at something. Instead I’m fucking around with a program that needs updating, or something that’s stopped working with something else, or a printer that needs six hundred dollars’ worth of ink and also says to me, “I’m sorry, I can no longer work for you until you install a new maintenance cartridge.”

It wore me down. It didn’t feel very human to me.

With collodion, I still like being there, doing it. For me, you just can’t beat that.

It is said that you store your plates in the attic, under a bed or in a closet; that there is no drive to exhibit, no drive to sell, only to make. What made this book exist?

G.B.: Jesse [Lenz, the founder of Charcoal Press] said he’d like to do a book and that I should send him some stuff to look at. We have known each other for years. Not super well. I’d see him once or twice a year when he came through Rockland. He has always been very enthusiastic and supportive of my work, even before my first two books were published.

Jesse saw me two years ago at a coffee shop I go to often and told me he was finally ready to do the “Definitive Gary Briechle” book. This coincided with me being at a certain stage and having all the stuff around the house, practically all of it has never been seen, and it’s started to feel like a bit of a bummer, so I thought this would be great, to do this book at this point, to get some of these things out in the world.

I really like the people I photograph. There’s a lot of people I know really well, literally for over 20 years, and I knew they would get a kick out of seeing themselves in a book.

A big obstacle for me is trying to talk about my work. Not a whole lot to talk about in a way. I think things can exist purely visually and that could be that. And I’m not much of a networker. I like left field where you watch the game more than you play it.

Everyone I take a portrait of, I make a print for the person who is in it. Those are like little micro exhibits. The person sees themselves, their girlfriend sees them, their mom and dad and some friends might see them. So in a way I’ve had a whole hell of a lot of micro exhibits over the last 30 years, and that feels so awesome, to give people pictures.

I think exhibiting once in a while feels good. You’re able to say to your mom and dad, “Hey, look, I’m not completely nuts.” But I think the networking, smooshing, inflated art talking about work feels not as good as doing the work.

And to me, the book is the ultimate exhibit. So I feel very happy and fortunate that Jesse is doing the book. And it’s a BIG book. If I can, I have a book going every 8 to 10 years or so, and that’s plenty.

It’s funny. The boxes of glass plates are extremely heavy. Often 80 or 90 5×7 plates in a small box, usually wooden, standing vertically. It never feels right to put them all on one series of shelves or in one place. They’re just too freaking heavy, so I put them all over the house. Kind of spreading the weight around.

Pulling things out for Jesse kind of drove me nuts because I’m like a stranger to my own work and I don’t know where it is. I don’t know what’s in the boxes. It’s frustrating, but it was also kind of fun. Like, oh yeah, I remember that one. Jesse said he liked that we were both seeing images for the first time together.

I guess I do what I wanna do. It’s a preference. It’s not much of a choice between things like networking, talking, doing gallery stuff and actually doing the work.

I guess I just like to actually do the work. I really really like to do the work. It’s a way of life.

No lighthouse appears anywhere in this book, and yet the title stands: I Want To See A Lighthouse , drawn from a child’s wish. Why this title, for these images?

G.B.: With photography, you have a relationship with the world. You’re not on your own. You’re responding to what’s around you. It begins with recognition: there is something here worth looking at, worth taking time to consider.

Years ago, I found a child’s notebook on the floor of the dump store in Rockland. That’s where people leave things they think someone else might want, and other people come to see what they can use. I don’t know whose notebook it was. On one page were the words, “I want to see a lighthouse.” And it was part of a hangman game.

Maine has a rocky coast, often hidden in fog. There are lighthouses everywhere. We’ve come to think of them as decorations—pictures on calendars and coffee mugs. It’s easy to forget what they were there for. Someone out on the water, in danger, needed to see a light. They needed a path into a safe harbor.

I think we all need that now. Sometimes it feels as though the whole world does. The stakes are really high.

But the sentence in the notebook was part of a game of hangman. In the upper left corner, you can see the little figure, partly drawn. That changes the words for me. There is still a chance to find the lighthouse, but there aren’t many guesses left. You need to find it while there’s still time. And this is by a child. A child wants to find a lighthouse. What does this say about the anxiety we instill in our children?

When you turn the page, there’s another sheet of ruled paper, shaded with dark pencil. The black is closing in around the white. I don’t know what the child intended, or whether the two pages had anything to do with each other. But I can’t help seeing them together.

To me, they carry the same feeling: there is still light, and only so much time to find it.

Your work has sometimes been set alongside that of Ralph Eugene Meatyard, for its sense of the uncanny, or Diane Arbus, for the frontality of her gaze and her recurring twins. I would add Roger Ballen, for the childlike drawings, the bones, the dark black-and-white world. Are there artists, be they photographers, painters or writers, whose work in particular inspires you?

G.B.: Diane Arbus is the big one for me. I’m very familiar with her monograph, the Revelations book and the book Untitled . I like her writings in the Revelations book. You could see the mania in the way she wrote a list. I relate to that. Her quotes in the monograph are some of the best words ever written about photography in my opinion. She is the quintessential example of what being “all in” means.

When I first saw her work, I didn’t get it in terms of how she made this picture. But over time I have developed a visual for it: she’s on a train going somewhere by herself. There is a train running parallel to her filled with people. For some reason very, very briefly the trains stop on the platform, both doors open and she sees into it, to the people. Really only for a blink of an eye. Then the door is closed and the trains move on. I have the sense of a wink or a blink, but she’s there with her camera and she has access to this parallel world. I remember thinking, “I want to see that world,” and I had no idea how to do it.

Over time I got a couple glimpses into it. It’s still a mystery, but I know it can happen. Most of what I make is crap, like beyond embarrassing crap, let’s put it at 98%. But I do get moments of the doors opening. That’s all you need.

There is a purity about Arbus. I really admire her. I know truth is a word that is maligned in photography. It’s like a joke, it’s so obvious that photography is not truthful. I guess, like, if you said on a test at Yale, “Diane Arbus tells the truth,” it would drag your score down a bit, but unquestionably for me there’s a personal and psychological truth in her work that’s beyond criticism.

Disfarmer is outwardly so plain, but unparalleled sensitivity. I like Eggleston a ton, he’s quirky. Well seen images. He is the definition of all in. Mark Cohen, what he does on the street is so affecting. Seems like the doors on the train open for him a lot.

I Want To See A Lighthouse by Gary Briechle is published by Charcoal Press , 2026. Hardcover, linen with a tipped-in image, 224 pages, 11 × 14 inches, $85.

title_original: Prima dell’opera: il senso del processo artistico nei contesti di cura
editorial_title_zh: 作品诞生之前：艺术创作过程在疗愈语境中的意义
editorial_excerpt_zh: 从 FarmaCrea 2026 活动期间浮现的主题出发，对创作过程、艺术语言、心理健康与疗愈路径之间的关系进行反思。本文《作品诞生之前：艺术创作过程在疗愈语境中的意义》源自 exibart.com。

2026。文章认为，艺术不能替代治疗，但可以与之并行，为那些难以找到词汇表达的内心体验提供一种语言。我对此表示赞同，并想补充一笔活动报道所遗漏的内容：在艺术经验成为一件图像、一件作品、一个故事之前，究竟发生了什么。", "links": [{"text": "exibart ha raccontato FarmaCrea 2026", "url": Campoli）的素描和米歇尔·OZ（Michel OZ）的装置作品《Black Brain》是源于个人探索的艺术家作品。唐·路易吉·迪列格罗基金会（Fondazione Don Luigi Di Liegro）的摄影作品《罗马壁画》（Murales di Roma）和《罗马房屋的窗户》（Le finestre delle case di Roma）则来自与接受疗愈路径的年轻人共同开展的工作坊。如果说先前的报道将这两种不同的状态联系在了一起，那么本文将探讨这些图像诞生语境之间的差异。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/farmacrea-2026-2.jpg", "对于工作坊的摄影作品而言，这种解读并非显而易见。诞生于疗愈语境中的图像未必就是自白或症状。它是抉择与环境的结果，人们可以在不立刻破译它的情况下对其进行观看和分享。在这些语境中，风险在于，甚至在倾听一个人之前，就将心理学意义归于他所做的事情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了项目和创作出的图像本身，还有必要深入了解工作坊的引导方式以及操作人员的角色。这是一个重要的区别：开放式工作坊、教育活动和艺术治疗干预是不同的实践，具有不同的目标和责任。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "物质与我们共同决定", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "人们常常将表达想象成一种已经成型的、寻求媒介的内在内容。在实践中，情况并非如此。一张被撕破的纸、一片意料之外晕染开的色彩、一块染上斑点的织物：物质设定了条件，而创作者必须做出回应。人们在边做边决定的过程中，发现了一些最初并未预料到的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我看来，艺术创作的独特性也体现在这里：它与一个会做出反应并参与过程发展的物质进行对话。每一个手势都会留下一个可见的效果，而这只能通过另一个手势来修改。在任何人对其进行解读之前，创作者就已经处于自身决定后果的关系之中。并非每项手工活动因此都具有治疗作用，我也不赋予物质它所不具备的力量。但当我们在社会卫生服务中谈论艺术时，这一独特性是必须予以考量的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/farmacrea-2026.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Farmacrea 2026", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "创作的时间", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "观察、收集、挑选、裁剪、并置、舍弃、重新开始。这些都是简单的手势，需要时间和决断。在集体中还会增添其他动作：索要材料、等待轮到自己、看着邻座的做法来改变选择。关系也诞生于这些日常行动之中，而不仅仅是在作品完成后的意义分享中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "创作的时间还提供了一种不必直接讲述自己的可能性。注意力转移到了一种颜色、一个手势的节奏、一个正在变化的表面上。从这个意义上说，治疗并不是改善的承诺，也不是更高自我觉察的承诺。它同样也是能够在一种不知结果的活动中停留，并通过共同的劳作与他人相遇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "未曾显形之物", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "文章在结尾时提醒我们，并非所有重要的事情都能立竿见影地被看到。我要补充的是，并非所有重要的事情都必须变得显形。一个过程即便没有带来一件完成的作品、即便结果依然不确定、即便创作者觉得无需解释，它也同样可以具有价值。重复的手势、变化的物质、重新拾起的决定、共同度过的时间都是体验的一部分，而不是它的边缘。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "将注意力从作品转移到过程，并不意味着放弃解读。这意味着人们认识到：意义并不总是先于创作而存在；有时它在劳作时形成，有时则保持开放。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果在疗愈语境中对艺术的叙述只展示作品，那么它就失去了意义的一半。谁来引导、使用什么方法、过程中发生了什么：这些信息和展出的图像一样，都是叙述中不可或缺的部分。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
In occasione della Giornata mondiale della salute mentale, exibart ha raccontato FarmaCrea 2026 , la serata promossa da MondoFarmacia al MACRO di Roma. Nell’articolo si sostiene che l’arte non sostituisce le cure ma può affiancarle, offrendo un linguaggio a vissuti che faticano a trovare le parole. Concordo e vorrei aggiungere ciò che un resoconto di evento lascia fuori: che cosa accade prima che un’esperienza artistica diventi un’immagine, un’opera, un racconto.

Il percorso espositivo teneva insieme elementi diversi. I disegni di Daniele Campoli e l’installazione Black Brain di Michel OZ sono lavori d’artista, nati da una ricerca personale. Le fotografie della Fondazione Don Luigi Di Liegro, Murales di Roma e Le finestre delle case di Roma , vengono invece da laboratori con giovani inseriti in percorsi di cura. Se nel resoconto si mettevano in relazione questi due differenti statuti, qui ci soffermiamo sulle differenze tra i contesti in cui queste immagini sono nate.

Per le fotografie dei laboratori questa lettura è la meno scontata. Un’immagine nata in un contesto di cura non è per forza una confessione o un sintomo. È il risultato di scelte e circostanze e si può guardare e condividere senza decifrarla subito. Il rischio, in questi contesti, è attribuire un significato psicologico a ciò che una persona ha fatto prima ancora di ascoltarla.

Al di là dei progetti e delle immagini realizzate, è necessario anche approfondire le modalità di conduzione dei laboratori e il ruolo degli operatori. È una distinzione rilevante: un laboratorio aperto, un’attività educativa e un intervento di arteterapia sono pratiche diverse, con obiettivi e responsabilità diversi.

La materia decide insieme a noi

Si immagina spesso l’espressione come un contenuto interiore già formato che cerca un mezzo. Nella pratica accade altro. Un foglio che si strappa, un colore che si allarga più del previsto, un tessuto che prende la tintura a macchie: la materia pone condizioni, e chi lavora deve rispondere. Si decide mentre si fa, e ciò che si scopre non era previsto all’inizio.

A mio avviso, una specificità del fare artistico risiede anche in questo: nel confronto con una materia che reagisce e che partecipa allo sviluppo del processo. Ogni gesto lascia un effetto visibile, che si può modificare soltanto attraverso un altro gesto. La persona si trova in rapporto con le conseguenze delle proprie decisioni prima che qualcuno le interpreti. Non ogni attività manuale è per questo terapeutica e non attribuisco alla materia poteri che non ha. Ma è una specificità che va considerata quando si parla di arte nei servizi socio-sanitari.

Il tempo del fare

Osservare, raccogliere, scegliere, ritagliare, accostare, scartare, ricominciare. Sono gesti semplici, che richiedono tempo e decisione. In gruppo se ne aggiungono altri: chiedere un materiale, aspettare il proprio turno, cambiare una scelta guardando ciò che fa il vicino. La relazione nasce anche da queste azioni ordinarie, non solo dalla condivisione dei significati a lavoro finito.

Il tempo del fare offre anche la possibilità di non dover raccontare direttamente se stessi. L’attenzione va a un colore, al ritmo di un gesto, a una superficie che cambia. In questo senso la cura non è la promessa di un miglioramento né di una maggiore consapevolezza di sé. È anche poter restare in un’attività senza conoscerne l’esito e incontrare altri attraverso un fare comune.

Ciò che non diventa visibile

L’articolo si chiude ricordando che non tutto ciò che conta si vede subito. Aggiungo che non tutto ciò che conta deve diventare visibile. Un processo può avere valore anche quando non porta a un’opera compiuta, quando l’esito resta incerto, quando chi l’ha fatto non sente il bisogno di spiegarlo. Il gesto che si ripete, la materia che cambia, la decisione ripresa, il tempo passato insieme sono parte dell’esperienza, non il suo contorno.

Spostare l’attenzione dall’opera al processo non significa rinunciare a interpretare. Significa riconoscere che il significato non precede sempre il fare: a volte si forma mentre si lavora, a volte resta aperto.

Un racconto dell’arte nei contesti di cura che mostri soltanto le opere ne perde metà. Chi conduce, con quale metodo, che cosa accade durante: sono informazioni che appartengono al racconto quanto le immagini esposte.

editorial_title_zh: 《一手更接近天空》。希拉帕·古普塔在米兰
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在米兰GAM，语言成为自由的空间：随着希拉帕·古普塔的《一手更接近天空》展览，由布鲁娜·罗卡萨瓦拉策划，由富莱拉基金会和GAM联合举办，展览将持续至2027年1月6日。文章《一手更接近天空。希拉帕·古普塔…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "当语言不再仅仅是一种交流工具，而成为一个被边界、禁令、归属和可能性所穿越的地方时，会发生什么？这是希拉帕·古普塔研究中提出的问题之一，这位印度艺术家是国际当代艺术界最具权威的声音之一，是GAM——米兰现代艺术画廊第八届富莱拉系列展的主角。古普塔在过去二十多年里一直致力于研究社会构建和规范身份的一些装置。语言、审查、流动性、边界和个体自由贯穿她的实践，根据所面对的问题，她的作品形式不断变化。雕塑、灯光装置、视频、声音和表演成为观察个体与集体、私人体验与公共空间之间关系的工具。她的作品诞生于这些维度重叠的区域，在那里，一个词、一幅图像或一个动作在不同的地方被说出或展示时，可能会有不同的意义。", "links": [{"text": "Furla Series", "url": "https://www.fondazionefurla.org/"}, {"text": "GAM – Galleria d’Arte Moderna", "url": "https://www.gam-milano.com/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Shilpa-Gupta-2-853x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "富莱拉系列——希拉帕·古普塔。《一手更接近天空》，2026年。由富莱拉基金会和GAM——米兰现代艺术画廊联合举办的展览现场。摄影：安德烈亚·罗塞蒂。版权：富莱拉基金会", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在米兰GAM美术馆，这种研究与一座历史悠久的建筑和永久收藏品展开对话，这种对比催生了一系列专门为博物馆位于皇家花园中的空间创作的新作品。该项目因此将一组作品带到米兰，这些作品概括了古普塔实践中的核心主题，构建了一条将环境维度提升为艺术体验不可或缺部分的路线。一件名为《I Live Under Your Sky Too》的作品，始于2004年，至今仍在进行中，仅从标题就能体现出艺术家研究中反复出现的张力。一句简单、几乎日常的句子引出了归属感和共存的问题：共享同一片天空是否真的意味着共享同一片空间、同样的权利、同样的行动自由和被认可的可能性？古普塔经常探讨这种表面上的普遍性与实际限制条件之间的差距。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Shilpa-Gupta-3-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Furla Series – Shilpa Gupta. One Palm Closer to the Sky, 2026. 由Fondazione Furla和GAM – 米兰现代艺术美术馆共同举办的展览现场。摄影：Andrea Rossetti。版权：Fondazione Furla", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，语言成为一种需要检验的材料。词语可以穿越领土，创造社群，标示差异，但也可以成为控制的工具。审查不仅涉及被明确禁止的内容，还涉及社会如何规定什么可以被说、由谁说、用哪种语言以及在何种空间中说。这是古普塔研究中特别深入探讨的领域，她将不同的语言和地理联系在一起，而不将政治维度与个人维度区分开来。展览的开场房间具有象征意义。一件特定场地的声学装置，由石头、家具和回收玻璃杯制成，将房间的复制品转化为一个共鸣箱。《When the Stone Sang to the Glass》以一种合唱和低语的方式演绎了《Bella Ciao》，将参观者带入这位印度艺术家的艺术和政治视野。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览继续展出名为《真相》的霓虹灯装置，其中文字被倒置。古普塔将观众的注意力引向当下的矛盾，以及当代社会面临的极权主义威胁和日益加剧的专制倾向。在这一背景下，艺术家探讨了审查制度、语言的核心地位以及政府对媒体的控制，她通过《SoundOnMySkin》等作品表达这些主题，这是一组旋转字母的显示屏，它否定了作为传递清晰信息媒介的自身角色，反而提供了混乱和脱节的句子。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Shilpa-Gupta-5-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Furla Series – Shilpa Gupta. One Palm Closer to the Sky, 2026. 由Fondazione Furla和GAM – 米兰现代艺术博物馆联合举办的展览现场。摄影：Andrea Rossetti。版权：Fondazione Furla", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在两件作品中，语言成为被调查的对象。这是民主的第一道防线，如今比以往任何时候都更被政府和政权用作引导日益受到当前挑战困扰的人民的工具。在展览中还包括互动装置如《Stand, Speak, Here》（2026年创作）和《Breathe》，通过不同的方式，邀请参观者直接与之互动。前者敦促观众站在砖块上并用闭唇发出声音，这明显指的是政治言论中对异议的边缘化和镇压。后者则呼吁参观者采取行动，提供机会让参观者通过将纸张放在博物馆墙壁上艺术家刻蚀的凹槽上，然后用粉笔描摹。在刻蚀的场景中，很快就能注意到被逮捕示威者的缺失。古普塔故意只展示执法者或暴徒的形象，而异议者的轮廓则仅通过他们缺席的回声出现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/Shilpa-Gupta-6-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Furla Series – Shilpa Gupta. One Palm Closer to the Sky, 2026. 由Fondazione Furla和GAM – 米兰现代艺术博物馆联合举办的展览现场。摄影：Andrea Rossetti。版权：Fondazione Furla", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "GAM的项目是在2021年起，Furla基金会与米兰博物馆之间建立的合作关系中诞生的。每年，这种合作都会推出一场全新的展览，旨在让当代艺术家的研究与GAM的历史环境和其收藏进行对话。这种对比使人们能够通过时间与文化上的距离来阅读作品，这种距离将它们与博物馆内保存的作品分隔开来。Furla Series由Furla基金会于2017年发起，并与意大利的重要艺术机构合作，推出了来自世界各地女性艺术家的个人展览，并有助于提升当代文化中女性主角的可见度。此次在米兰与Shilpa Gupta的相遇，是其国际广泛艺术研究的一部分。从威尼斯双年展到柏林、沙迦、利物浦和光州双年展，再到欧洲、亚洲和美国博物馆的展览，这位艺术家的作品跨越了不同的背景，始终将个体、领土和权力结构之间的关系作为核心。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Cosa accade quando il linguaggio smette di essere soltanto uno strumento per comunicare e diventa un luogo attraversato da confini, divieti, appartenenze e possibilità? È una delle domande che accompagnano la ricerca di Shilpa Gupta , artista indiana tra le voci più autorevoli della scena contemporanea internazionale, protagonista dell’ottava edizione di Furla Series alla GAM – Galleria d’Arte Moderna di Milano. Gupta lavora da oltre vent’anni su alcuni dei dispositivi attraverso cui le società costruiscono e regolano l’identità. Linguaggio, censura, mobilità, confini e libertà individuale attraversano una pratica che cambia forma a seconda delle domande affrontate. Sculture, installazioni luminose, video, suono e performance fungono da strumenti per osservare il rapporto tra individuo e collettività, esperienza privata e spazio pubblico. Il suo lavoro nasce proprio dove queste dimensioni si sovrappongono, in quella zona in cui una parola, un’immagine o un gesto possono assumere significati diversi a seconda del luogo in cui vengono pronunciati o mostrati.

Alla GAM, questa ricerca viene messa in dialogo con un edificio storico e una collezione permanente, un confronto che ha dato origine a una serie di nuove produzioni realizzate appositamente per gli spazi del museo sito negli splendidi Giardini della Villa Reale. Il progetto porta dunque a Milano una selezione di opere che sintetizza alcuni dei nuclei centrali della pratica di Gupta , costruendo un percorso in cui la dimensione ambientale viene elevata a parte integrante dell’esperienza artistica. Un’opera come I Live Under Your Sky Too , iniziata nel 2004 e tuttora in corso, restituisce già nel titolo una delle tensioni ricorrenti nella ricerca dell’artista. Una frase semplice, quasi quotidiana, introduce una questione di appartenenza e convivenza: condividere lo stesso cielo vuole dire davvero condividere lo stesso spazio, gli stessi diritti, la stessa possibilità di muoversi e di essere riconosciuti? Gupta lavora spesso proprio su questo scarto tra ciò che appare come universale e le condizioni concrete che ne limitano l’accesso.

Il linguaggio si fa così materia da mettere alla prova. Le parole possono attraversare territori, creare comunità, segnare differenze, ma anche diventare strumenti di controllo. La censura riguarda sia ciò che viene esplicitamente proibito ma anche i modi in cui una società stabilisce cosa può essere detto, da chi, in quale lingua e in quale spazio. È un terreno particolarmente sondato nella ricerca di Gupta , che mette in relazione lingue e geografie diverse senza separare la dimensione politica da quella intima. La sala che apre la mostra è in questo senso emblematica. Un’installazione sonora site-specific, realizzata con pietre, arredi e bicchieri di recupero trasforma la riproduzione di una stanza in una cassa di risonanza. When the Stone Sang to the Glass si traduce in una versione corale e sussurrata di “Bella Ciao” che proietta il visitatore nella visione artistica e politica dell’artista indiana.

La mostra prosegue con l’installazione Truth , neon in cui la scritta viene rovesciata. Gupta porta all’attenzione di chi osserva le contraddizioni del presente, le tensioni di una contemporaneità che assiste alla minaccia del ritorno dei totalitarismi e alle derive autoritarie che si fanno strada sempre più insistentemente. In questo contesto, l’artista tratta tematiche quali censura, centralità del linguaggio e controllo dei media operato dai governi e lo fa con opere come SoundOnMySkin , display a lettere rotanti che sconfessa il proprio ruolo di mezzo indicato per dotare le persone di informazioni chiare e, invece, fornisce frasi sconnesse, confuse.

In entrambe le opere, è il linguaggio ad essere indagato. Primo baluardo delle democrazie che, oggi più che mai, è utilizzato da governi e regimi come mezzo per orientare popoli sempre più provati dalle sfide del presente. Nel percorso figurano anche installazioni interattive quali Stand, Speak, Here (realizzata nel 2026) e Breathe che, tramite modalità differenti, invitano i visitatori a confrontarsi direttamente con esse. La prima ci esorta a salire su dei mattoni ed emettere un suono con le labbra chiuse, chiaro riferimento alla marginalizzazione e alla repressione del dissenso nel discorso politico. La seconda chiama invece all’azione il visitatore, a cui viene offerta la possibilità di realizzare un frottage appoggiando un foglio di carta sulle incisioni fatte dall’artista su una parete del museo per poi ricalcare con il pastello. Nelle scene incise si nota subito la mancanza dei manifestanti arrestati. Gupta mostra deliberatamente solo le figure delle forze dell’ordine o degli abusanti, mentre i profili dei dissidenti compaiono solo attraverso l’eco della loro assenza.

Il progetto della GAM nasce all’interno di una collaborazione che dal 2021 lega Fondazione Furla e il museo milanese. Ogni anno la partnership produce una mostra inedita pensata per far dialogare la ricerca di un’artista contemporanea con gli ambienti storici della GAM e con la sua collezione. È un confronto che permette di leggere le opere anche attraverso la distanza, temporale e culturale, che le separa dalle opere conservate nel museo. Furla Series , avviato nel 2017 da Fondazione Furla in collaborazione con importanti istituzioni artistiche italiane, ha dato vita a mostre personali di artiste da tutto il mondo e ha contribuito a offrire visibilità alle donne protagoniste della cultura contemporanea. L’appuntamento milanese con Shilpa Gupta si inserisce in una ricerca artistica di ampio respiro internazionale. Dalla Biennale di Venezia alle biennali di Berlino, Sharjah, Liverpool e Gwangju, fino alle mostre nei musei di Europa, Asia e Stati Uniti, il lavoro dell’artista ha attraversato contesti diversi mantenendo sempre al centro il rapporto tra individuo, territorio e strutture di potere.

イギリスの美術市場は30年でどう変化したのか？ 最新レポートが示す成長と停滞

世界第2位の規模を誇る イギリス の美術市場は、過去30年間でどのような変化を遂げたのか。業界団体BAMFの最新レポートは、金融危機後の市場の回復状況に加え、ギャラリーやオークション市場の現状、国際的な競争力などを明らかにしている。

ブリティッシュ・アート・マーケット・フェデレーション（BAMF）は、過去30年間における イギリス の美術市場の動向を分析した市場レポート「The British Art Market 1996–2025」を 発表した 。同報告書では、市場規模の推移や経済効果を検証するとともに、主要な競争相手であるアメリカや中国との比較を行っている。このレポートは、 アート・バーゼル と UBS が手がけるマーケットレポートなども担当する、Arts Economicsによって執筆された。

イギリス美術市場の成長と課題

報告書によれば、イギリスの美術市場は取引額において世界第2位の市場規模を依然として誇っている。売上高は1996年の26億ポンド（現在の為替レートで約5465億円、以下同）から、2025年には80億ポンド（1兆6811億円）へと成長を遂げた。ただし、この増加には物価上昇の影響も含まれており、実質的な成長幅は数字ほど大きくない。

過去30年間でイギリスの美術市場が最大規模に達したのは2008年で、売上高は112億ポンド（約2兆3541億円）を記録した。しかし、世界金融危機の影響で市場は急激に縮小し、翌2009年には57億ポンド（約1兆2000億円）とほぼ半減した。

一方、金融危機後の市場の回復が鈍いことは、懸念点の一つとして挙げられる。2009年以降、イギリスの美術市場の売上高は約40％増加したものの、2025年時点でも金融危機前の水準には回復していない。BAMFのプレジデント、アンソニー・ブラウンは報告書のなかで、同連盟に所属する多くの小規模事業者が、過剰で増え続ける規制によって事業活動が圧迫されていると訴えていることを指摘した。なお、報告書で2020年のイギリスのEU離脱（ブレグジット）に言及しているのは、報告手続きの変更に伴う2021年以降のEUからの輸入増加について説明した箇所だけだ。

2025年のイギリスの美術市場は、ヨーロッパ全体の約半分を占め、他国を大きく引き離して域内最大の市場となった。また、世界全体の取引額に占める割合は18％で、フランスの8％や中国の14％を上回ったものの、44％を占めるアメリカには大きく差をつけられている。

2025年の美術品輸入額は2015年と比較して45％減少したが、2000年と比べると35％増えている。一方、輸出額は2000年比で46％増加したものの、2025年は前年比15％減となった。この輸出額の減少について報告書は、ドナルド・トランプ大統領が関税をめぐる方針をたびたび変更したことによる「間接的な影響や先行きの不透明感」が背景にあった可能性を指摘している。実際、輸出額の減少の大部分は、対米輸出が落ち込んだことによるものだった。しかし、長期的に見ると、イギリスの美術品取引におけるアメリカへの依存度は低下している。2000年以降、輸出額全体に占める対米輸出の割合は半減し、輸入額全体に占めるアメリカからの輸入の割合もほぼ同程度減少した。

ギャラリー経営の実態

報告書によると、2025年時点でイギリスには約7610の美術商やギャラリーがあり、その約3分の1が ロンドン に集中している。売上高は推計46億ポンド（約9668億円）に上り、事業者数は2003年から約3分の1増加した。その大半は「小規模または零細事業者」で、2025年の売上高が100万ポンド（約2億1020万円）以下の事業者が全体の89％を占めている。

アートフェアはギャラリー経営において重要な役割を果たしており、2025年には美術商の売上高全体の37％を占めた。一方、イギリス国内で開催されたアートフェアは2019年の52件から2025年には40件強に減少している。また、ギャラリーはアートフェアへの参加に多額の費用を投じており、2025年の支出総額は約3億1500万ポンド（約661億円）に上った。

ギャラリーの売上高は、一部の作家に集中する傾向がある。2025年には、最も売上の多い作家1人が平均38％、上位3人では59％を占めた。こうした傾向は年々強まっており、上位3人の割合は2022年の48％から59％へと上昇した。ただし、これはイギリスに限った現象ではなく、世界全体でも上位3人の作家が占める割合は51％から58％に増えている。

オークション市場の取引動向

美術品や骨董品、その他の収集品を扱うオークションハウスも、イギリスの美術市場で大きな存在感を示す。国内にある約3500の競売業者・オークション会場のうち、こうした商品を扱う1170のオークションハウスが、2025年の市場全体の取引額の42％にあたる33億ポンド（約7000億円）を売り上げた。この金額は前年比8％増となったものの、過去最高を記録した2023年と比べると20％低い水準だ。また、落札された美術品の78％は5000ドル（約80万円）未満だった一方、100万ドル以上で落札された作品は全体の1％にも満たなかった。しかし、取引額では100万ドル以上の作品が全体の55％を占め、うち100万〜1000万ドル（約1億5800万〜15億8000万円）の価格帯だけで取引額全体の45％に達した。

オークション市場で最大の割合を占めるのは、戦後から現代にかけて制作された美術作品で、取引額全体の半分弱に相当する。一方、オールドマスターの市場ではイギリスが世界をリードし、世界全体のオールドマスター作品の取引額の38％を占めた。また、イギリスの美術市場が2025年にもたらした税収は、少なく見積もっても15億ポンド（約3152億円）に上るという。（翻訳：編集部）

CHURA VITA チュラ・ヴィータ

劇場公開日： 2026年11月6日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

U-NEXTで 関連作品を見る PR

解説・あらすじ

沖縄を拠点に作品を撮り続けてきた「HAPPY SANDWICH」の岸本司監督が、世界有数の長寿地域「ブルーゾーン」として知られる沖縄・やんばるを舞台に、スウェーデンから訪れた1人の女性の目を通して「よりよく生きるとは何か」を見つめるヒューマンドラマ。沖縄北部・やんばるの豊かな自然や、伝統の木造帆船サバニ、琉球染織に息づく「生きる知恵」を織り込んで描く。 長寿地域「ブルーゾーン」沖縄の秘密に惹かれたニコリーナは、特別な生き方を探し求めてスウェーデンから島へ渡る。だが理想郷のイメージの奥で、古くから受け継がれてきた食文化や祈り、繊細な手仕事が近代化の波の中で少しずつ姿を消しつつあった。守られてきた営みが薄れていく姿を前に、彼女は自分をこの地へ導いた問いを見失っていく。そんな折、海岸に打ち上げられた1頭のイルカと出会い、声なき命を海へ返そうとする時間の中で、「生きること」の重みと自然への畏敬を静かに教えられていく。 主人公ニコリーナを演じるのは、実際に沖縄を訪れたスウェーデン人のニコリーナ・スベンセン。 城間やよい、真栄城興和、満名匠吾らが共演する。

true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "治疗一开始似乎像个奇迹，但结果却难以预测。马特的皮肤开始变形，他的面部失去稳定性，他的身体发展出了超出了科学控制范围的能力。最初为了找回身份而进行的绝望搜寻，逐渐演变成一场身体和心理上的噩梦，吞噬着主角以及他周围的每一个人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "你可能感兴趣", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "极端场景赋予了点睛之笔", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当制作团队专注于马特的身体以及几乎帮不上忙的治疗后果时，它展现出了自己的实力。这部电影并不满足于暗示畸形：它展示了割伤、紧绷的皮肤、被改造的组织以及不再听从主人意志的面孔。这是一种物理上的、令人不适的恐怖，对于习惯了其他DC作品的观众来说，视觉上刻意令人反感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "沃金斯在主角试图控制一场扬言要吞噬他的变形的那些镜头中找到了最佳时刻。在一场飞机上的戏中，马特一边与开始遮住他眼睛的皮肤作斗争，一边又有湍流让每一个动作都变得复杂，这场戏集成了该片的大部分优点：张力、视觉冲击力以及一种迫使人们透过手指缝看银幕的残酷感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中还融入了复仇叙事。它构建了荒诞的情境，并利用周围人的身份进行游戏，直到迎来一个夜间序列，该序列利用面孔的变换来成倍放大暴力与混乱。\\u201c泥面人\\u201d毫无保留地拥抱了其最疯狂的一面，并迸发出了在剧本其余部分并非总能保持的能量。沃金斯明白，这个角色的恐怖并不单单取决于将他变成一个怪物般的生物，而是要展示一个看似正常的外表如何能够变成无法辨认的模样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "当故事需要推进时便会失去力量的怪物", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "问题在于，当电影想要超越其恐怖设定时。第一部分颇具耐心地构建了马特的绝望、他对找回失去的面孔的需求以及他与凯特琳建立的关系。这种维度使得人们能够将该角色视作环境的受害者，一个在面对无法理解的变形时依然保留着部分人性的人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cinefilosoficial.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/image-2026-07-22T121500.661-1024x547.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Cinéfilos", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "两人之间的关系也引入了一种浪漫而悲剧的成分。马特在女科学家身上找到了可能的救赎，而她则在她的病人身上看到了一个证明此前一直被边缘化的研究价值的机会。然而，他们之间的吸引力使这种联系变得复杂，并增添了一种电影未能以必要深度展开的张力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着马特发现新的能力并开始用它们来向伤害过他的人复仇，电影抛弃了它先前建立的部分规则。变形变得越来越不可预测，在某些段落中，它们似乎更多地是为了迎合动作戏的需求，而不是出于内在逻辑。结果是後半部分的一致性有所降低，视觉诡计和暴力场景占据了本可以用于对主角进行更复杂刻画的空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过侦探的视角展现的哥谭腐败、各受害者之间的警方追捕以及凯特琳的个人冲突提供了一些有趣的元素，但没有一个元素最终获得足够的分量来决定性地丰富核心冲突。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "献给DC的不同尝试", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《泥面人》（Clayface）的一大成功之处在于其决定作为一部独立故事运作。蝙蝠侠无需出场，故事便能在哥谭市找到其定位，而这部电影也不依赖于与其他DC宇宙项目的连续彩蛋或彩联动。它的下注在于从一个不同的视角探索反派，运用恐怖片的工具以及一个聚焦于身体与情感恶化的故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中也有一种针对娱乐产业对美感、外表和公众形象之执念的可能解读。马特在不再符合将他塑造成明星的身体理想时失去了自己的位置。他的蜕变将这种逻辑推向了极致：曾经为他打开所有大门的脸变成了一座监狱，而他对恢复原貌的需求最终将他推向了一个怪物般的身份。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "电影并没有对这些想法进行过多的挖掘，但其前提让它们得以浮现，而无需将叙事变成一则直白的讽刺。从这个意义上说，当它的恐怖元素得以自行发声时，其聚焦方式便显得更加引人入胜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cinefilosoficial.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/1790381341798-a1ay07-1024x670.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Cinéfilos", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《泥面人》（Clayface）远非一部非凡之作。它的剧本并不总能跟上其影像的冲击力，某些角色陷入了过于明显的职能中，且当主角开始施展其能力时，故事便失去了连贯性。但它最精彩的片段在超级英雄电影中提供了一些与众不同的东西：一种身体上的、令人不适且有时真正令人不安的体验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "评分：7/10。已于10月22日登陆各大院线。", "translated": true}]
